review:
Spare a thought for the small-time 40k developer. You put all this blood and tears into making a Grey Knight game, paying close attention to all the little details and giving all the little Grey Knights last names for them to dramatically shout out, only to have some jerk like me come along and say 'hey, wouldn't this whole premise work a lot better with the Deathwatch?' 

Anyhow, when people say this an XCom clone, they really mean it. The story's got the same basic character dynamics (wise advisor guy, grumpy engineer, angry monthly report man and sexy research babe), it's got the same overworld where you pass time and wait for missions and the exact same squad based combat. All they've really done is applied a Warhammer 40k layer of paint.

But is that so bad? 

It's been years since XCom 2 came out. There hasn't been a new Fire Emblem in a long time. I think I appreciated this just for scratching the tactical combat itch. I mean, sure, it isn't doing anything that XCom wasn't doing already. But I've beaten XCom 1 and 2 already, and even did the whole Long War thing, so I am sort of XCom'd out at this point. 

The combat does feel different than XCom though. These are the Emperor's Space Marines, which means that you can hug cover if you want to, but you can also just pray really hard and then stand out in the open and let whoever come at you who wants a piece. Everyone has psychic powers and gimmicks that let you lay the hurt on Nurgle's minions and make the Death Guard regret worshiping a living garbage can. I am really experienced with these kinds of games and found that the Hard difficulty kept a pretty consistent challenge going from start to finish. 

The story will probably be completely incomprehensible to anyone that isn't 40k literate. If the words 'Nurgle', 'Mortarian', 'Geneseed' or 'Immaterium' don't mean anything to you, then you should not expect to have any idea what these people are going on about or why beating up a bunch of fat green guys is the best way to combat an intergalactic pandemic. But even if you do know all of the first founding Legions by their numbers, the story is a fairly straightforward 40k affair. I enjoyed it and I actually quite liked the characters, but it's not at the level of the Dawn of War games or anything like that. 

The game does have some downsides, mainly: 

1) There are random FTL-style events on your space ship as you fly around, and some of them are total crap. One of these things involved the monthly report man asking me to destroy all my upgrade materials because they were tainted by Chaos. I told him no and he cut me off from 'the armory' for sixty in-game days, which resulted in me not getting any rewards for any missions in the last 30% of the game. I never got a Chaplain because of this. WELL GEE THANKS GRANDMASTER DICKFACE! 

2) Focusing only on Nurgle was kind of dull after a while. I would have liked to have seen more stuff from the other Chaos Gods. Also your guys always mention passing by Ultramarine forces, but you never talk to them. Sad. 

3) Some bugginess. Now before you get too amped up about that, I would actually say that this is LESS buggy than either XCom game. At no point did I have a someone try to shoot a giant mutant two squares away from him only to find that your guy can't see him. The most frequent bug was having abilities get greyed out improperly, but selecting another ability and then going back to the one I was using before fixed that. No big deal.  

4) The game doesn't allow mods, meaning that you can't add Tau Crisis Suits or anime girls to your Grey Knight squads. :( 

5) No cameo appearance from Roboute Guilliman. :( 

Final rating: 8.924/11 Fists of the Emperor's Furah!

After beating the campaign, and before I jump into the next one to try and collect more achievements, I figured I'd leave a review.

First off:
This game is hard as balls, even for somebody familiar with the XCOM genre like me. I will attach four helpful tips at the end of this review which may make your life easier if you give the game a shot after reading this.

The game is also a bit janky in some regards, but in my opinion, it is the charming kind of jank.
Don't expect too grimdark serious business - this is not Space Marine, Mechanicus, or the like. Characters have a clear stereotype reference to the common tropes of the XCOM genre: The grumbly advisor, the smartass researcher gal, and the voice of reason techie. It's charming in a way though, and having a Grey Knight with a severe lisp and an Admech lady with an articulated monobrow is kinda fun. (Shoutout to Lunette, she was consistently my favourite of the trio.)

The VA is mostly solid, with some pretty good lines especially in cutscenes, and some of the enemy callouts are pretty good. This being said, the VA for the cultist enemies is /really/ bad, it completely misses the mark and doesn't sell the "mentally unhinged" stereotype well at all. It ends up extremely grating, and really harms the mood in any mission including them.

The enemy variety is actually surprisingly decent, despite being Nugle-only themed (like unfortunately many 40k games have). New enemies are often introduced without much fanfare mid-mission, but the "enemy attention triggered" cinematics that zoom in on them and give them a full animation make for some really good "oh crap" moments.  Often, what was up until then a fairly casual mission, suddenly turns into a lot of sweating and adrenaline as you try and deal with the new and completely unknown opponent, having to figure out its abilities on the fly. Pretty neat!

Overall, the game offers both plenty of well-known, tried and tested things of the genre: Turn-based fights (duh), cover mechanics, range mechanics, explodable environments, enemy behaviour variety, different firearms and (lots!) of melee weapons. 
But it also gives its own spin on some other things, like the many psychic powers, and the choice of equipment with Power armour or Terminator armour (which influence not only toughness, but also your pathing and movement options!), or some cover pieces you can strategically use to harm enemies (super fun!).
Also, the cinematics when you kick down a door are just too cool, made me grin every time.

So yeah! Overall, while definitely not up to par with some of the really grand 40k games, I would still recommend this game to anyone who is a 40k fan, and loves the XCOM genre, especially if you can pick it up on a sale.


NOW!
The promised "four tips to make your life easier", delivered at the end as promised:
1 - This is /not/ XCOM. You can switch between your characters at will during your turn, even after already doing some actions! Use this, and keep going back and forth as needed!
2 - Decide on a "balls to the wall" approach with just straight running in and dealing as much damage as you can asap, or a cautious one (with using the Aegis ability, and moving cover-to-cover). Once you picked, make sure to gear and skill your characters accordingly. Stay consistent. Do not try a middle ground between the two, it will not work well.
3 - A Librarian with teleport, or the Gate of Infinity stratagem are near mandatory. On things like the Bloom missions, you can use them to teleport your entire squad right next to the Bloom or a boss and immediately clap it, bypassing the entire boss room plus any reinforcement waves. It will be less XP than slogging it out, but saves you a looot of time and injury risks.
4 - Get a Purifier with grenades. No, seriously. Depending on tech level of your grenades and enemy level, these dudes can wipe an entire enemy patrol by tossing a krak and then one frag (make sure you do it in that order, as the frag has knockback). Using a Power Armour that gives bonuses to grenades as well as grenade talents will give you 3 of each. This means this mean guy can instantly nuke three enemy patrols all by himself, clearing the way to the main objective of any mission without breaking a sweat. I cannot stress enough the amount of damage these dudes do. I am pretty sure my two Purifiers got easily 75% of the kills of my entire campaign. Bring one of these battle bros anytime you can.

Well, after 120 hours and about 5 restarts, I've finally begun to figure out this game.

A lot has been said about the difficulty of Daemonhunters, a major criticism being that you don't feel like a storied "Grey Knight" of the Imperium, that is to say, the power fantasy of playing the elite of the Astartes isn't evident in the game play. Much of this can be solved by playing on the easiest difficulty, where chaos cultists and other fodder are dispatched quickly, and while not a breeze, won't frustrate you. Once you've learned the mechanics of the game, it really opens up to become very strategic and tactical. The encounters can be tense and epic, especially during some of the new missions in the DLC.

Once it all comes together, Daemonhunters is one of the best 40k games to have been released. It's not a power fantasy. This is a tale of desperation, which is a often overlooked 40k theme that is rarely touched upon but has always been lurking in the grim-dark universe we love. I appreciate the move away from comic book heroes to the a more authentic portrayal of the source material. Don't get me wrong, these are still bad ass Space Marines, larger than life and heroic in their bearing, but they're not invincible. Their duty is to sacrifice for the Emperor, and that they do. Only the Ordo Malleus could take on this challenge, and even then, victory is not assured.

If you're looking for a deep and challenging tactical combat game, with well thought out mechanics and progression, a good story with great presentation, and if you're never letting go of this 40k crap until the day you die, Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters is a worthy addition to you game library.

Honor the chapter, brothers. The Emperor protects.

Recommended.

I don't intended to write a review for this game, but after hesitating to buy it myself at first, when I saw so much negative reviews I finally bought it and now I've finished the game. And boy these negative reviewers are misleading either due to incompetence or due to spite, it's hard to tell. Mind you that I was playing on a normal difficulty, scared by all the reviews and game is not easy, don't get me wrong. However, I've finished my campaign with 0 (zero) marines/assassins ever being downed or killed, including boss fights and that, if you ask me, as far from 40k feeling as it gets, but was satisfying nevertheless. So, I will base my review on quotes from other reviews I saw just now and it can get pretty long, sorry about that. Also, I'll leave the comment section open for people I quote to get back on me:

- "the enemy will always injure your soldiers if they are alive at the end of a turn" - lies, in  a midgame they will barely get a chance to move. But to add some hints for cases when enemy is going to have a move next turn: 1) You can severe it's limb carrying it's most dangerous weapon 2) You can make it attack it's allies 3) you can create a killzone with "overwatch" and hazardous environment like fire so they will not reach you alive 4) focus on ranged troops and keeping distance with melee ones to finish them off next turn etc. 
Most importantly, HP threshold to be in the "wounded" states are much lower than XCOM, and adding the fact that you can boost your off-mission healing to +300%, your wounded marines will heal while being on route to the next mission. Don' t forget to use your Apothecary healing, Medicae skulls or play around armor. Also worth mentioning the augmentation mechanic that expects your marines  to be critically injured from time to time so they can be augmented during the recovery process. I don't like this mechanic btw, because I have never met this condition during my playthrough on normal

- "you do not have access to weapons or grenades that can efficiently do area damage and defeat large groups of enemies. That's right - the two ranged weapons with an AOE cone have very short range and don't do enough damage to take out even the weakest enemies with one volley, meaning that even if you expose your unit by moving into a favorable position, you will certainly be overwhelmed with attacks next turn." - wow, that must be a joke. There are selection of grenades and they are OP the whole game, I had a grenade focused Purifier with a flamer and he was like literally deleting chaos terminator squads in 2 throws during the final mission lol. Also, there are AoE abilities, too many to list them here. AoE firing modes, even for some melee weapons, I had 2 such melee AoE weapons during my playthrough and during the early stages of the game - a lot of environmental AoE objects like explosives, fuel tanks, statues, braziers, cranes with detachable cargo, all this will help you with crowd control

- "Unlike XCOM's two action points per turn, units in this game have three. For you that is almost irrelevant, since you need to usually save one to boost your armor to reduce the amount of damage you take turn after turn after turn. Having 3AP means the enemies, however, can move incredibly long distances to get into melee or flank you, always ensuring you take damage." - Baseline of action points(AP) is three, that is correct, but: 1) Boosting your armor is rarely a good AP use, excluding your tank characters 2) This game is almost built around increasing your AP through combat. There are a ton of abilities that are adding or refunding the AP. The first one you will probably see is execution (when humanoid enemy is stunned, melee attack will have an option to execute it giving +1 AP to EVERY marine, it can be further amplified by gear and abilities to give 2 or even 3 AP per execution per marine, yeah that crazy much), you can even build your squad around stuns/executions with access to advanced classes in a midgame like paladin and chaplain. Other honorable mentions are : "Honor the chapter" ability your first ever marine(Justicar) can unlock, crits with melee/ranged for some classes will refund AP (I had my Interceptor get 2 AP after melee crit that can trigger 2 times/turn, 1 AP refund after teleporting 2 times/turn), basically every class has ways of reducing AP cost or refunding AP, when meeting certain conditions, and one of the first stratagems is to give any marine +2AP. The list goes on.

- "enemies are always ridiculously much stronger than your squad on later stages of the game. In X-COM you are weak only at the beginning, when you do not have technologies, here you are always feel weak." - same as XCOM, mid-late game you have so much tools to use that, if built correctly, your squads will finish missions with enemies don't even scratching them

- "Games are about fun, not about frustration, when unbalanced difficulty spikes on normal (!) difficulty level just force you to witness constant failures of your squad even when you try to play carefully. I had never such experience even on hard level in X-COM." - it is hard to believe that XCOM veteran that played it on Hard can have not even a hard time but any form of a challenge on Normal difficulty in this game. I am not a hardcore XCOM/Tactical player and, again, I've finished my campaign without losses. Something that is not that easy to achieve in XCOM

I will cut this here, feel free to continue this discussion in a comments section, I think I made my point for the doubting people to at least give this game a try. It definitely deserves it despite a very valid list of flaws other reviewers have pointed out. But solid 40k/XCOM inspired games are too rare to be that picky, especially during deep sales. Have fun all!

[h1]Warhammer40K Chaos Gate - Save Scum Simulator[/h1]

[h2][u]Overview[/u][/h2]
[i]Warhammer 40K: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters[/i] (Chaos Gate) is a turn based tactical strategy that draws comparisons to the highly popular XCOM series. However, in addition to the Warhammer 40K flavor, it removes one of the biggest memes of XCOM – there is no random chance to hit. Both space marines and demons alike will always hit their mark. That’s right commander, you can’t blame your failures on a 99% chance to hit missing a crucial shot this time. 

[h2][u]Gameplay - Tactics[/u][/h2]
This game is not just a clone of XCOM nor does it feel like a Warhammer 40K mod for the game. Sure, the gameplay is similar. As the commander, you outfit squads to exterminate xenos scum while maintaining a headquarters in a careful balancing act of construction and research. However, that’s about where the similarities end. Overwatch is in the game, but it’s not nearly as powerful nor deadly as in XCOM. Relying on overwatch will not bring great glory. Instead, it pays off to be extremely aggressive – wipe out all the enemies before they can do any harm. This is done through various systems working together: action economy, critical hits, stuns, and executions.

Every member of the squad starts an encounter with 3 action points. This is used for both movement and attacking. A melee critical hit and certain special attacks (both melee and ranged) can lead to “precision targeting” which is a really fun feature. Essentially you can dismember an opponent to prevent an ability or certain attacks. This is especially useful in the early game where it may be more difficult to outright kill all enemies. Instead, they can be heavily neutered. Many enemies have both a ranged and melee option but heavily favor one or the other. Thus some enemies can become effectively harmless after missing a limb, allowing your squad some breathing room before they can clean up the mess next turn. However, especially in the later game, it may be worth using the precision targeting to stun an enemy quicker. After an enemy is stunned, the next hit is a guaranteed critical strike. The critical strike will also offer a new precision targeting option of “execution”. This leads to a brutal animation, but more importantly the entire squad gains a single action point. With some tactical thinking and good plays, encounters become more like puzzles of how to best spend actions to pull off executions in order to fuel more actions. When done correctly, the space marines should be able to quickly end an encounter without getting hurt. 

That said, defensive play is still an option with the cover system. Full cover pretty much guarantees will not get hurt unless flanked. Partial cover reduces damage. There is armor to help negate damage as well but it seems pretty unreliable as the enemy are servants of Nurgle. Plague is their friend, so they often just bypass armor to damage you with poison anyways.

What is also unfortunate is the battles get tedious and boring after 30-40 hours of it. I got my money’s worth but the replayability and drive to min-max isn’t there for me. The same few mission objectives repeat over and over – eventually even the maps do as well.


[h2][u]Story[/u][/h2]
While I enjoy Warhammer 40K, the extent of my knowledge comes from the games. I never played the board game nor do I read any of the novels. I researched the names that come up during the story of seemingly important characters and demons and they all seem to be well established in the lore. So that is pretty neat and maybe are some cool name drops for people who recognize the lore. To me, they are all just badasses and demons I need to murder though.

That said, there is a story and a reason you’re hunting demons – aside from it being your profession of course. The game follows a specific chapter of Space Marines called the Grey Knights. They are powerful psykers (users of psychic abilities – which comes to play in the gameplay as well, by the way!) who hunt demons. After a recent demon invasion, this particular group of marines are left limping when they are commandeered by the Inquisition to investigate a troublesome matter. Thus, the Grey Knights, led by you, and an Inquisitor join forces to uncover a Nurgle plot and work together how to cleanse its corruption from the system. 

[h2][u]Gameplay - Overworld[/u][/h2]
Here is where the other portion of the game takes place – outside of battles. You command your ship to fly planet to planet on a star grid. This is where you will find missions (battles) eventually. In between missions you are selecting construction, research, etc. You can also talk to NPCs aboard the ship which reminded me of Starcraft 2’s campaign. I enjoyed that aspect. When missions came up it is difficult, if not impossible, to reach all of them. They eventually run out on a timer. Thus as the commander you should assess which missions to tackle based on corruption level, proximity, and rewards. Rewards come in the form of requisition (currency), grimoires (research), or servitors (construction).

What I wasn’t a fan of was all the choices for random events that happened in between missions. The leader of the Grey Knights is kind of a dick. Most options you can take will end up pissing someone off. Thus you never really feel rewarded. Hell, even when the grandmaster rewarded me and asked me what I wanted it still felt like a punishment! I said I needed more gear and so as a reward all future mission for the next 60 days only rewarded requisition. Well, there goes all my construction efforts for the next 60 days. No servitors for me. 

[h2][u]Praises[/u][/h2]
-	Warhammer 40K game that is actually decent
-	Good gameplay mechanics (battles)
-	Decent Story

[h2][u]Criticisms[/u][/h2]
-	Developers making weird decisions (first week balance patch nerfing everything was WTF?)
-	Encourages save scumming with the terrible random events – or padding out the game more by having to deal with the negatives
-	The most fun classes locked behind a story event 
-	Terrible respec system that forces you to kill your own guys on purpose

[h2][u]Specs[/u][/h2]
I had to tone the game down to Medium otherwise the game seemed to crash to desktop at times.

Operating System: Windows 10
Processor (CPU): Intel Core i5-3570K CPU @3.40GHz
Graphics Card (GPU): NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070
Memory (RAM) 16 GB

[h2][u]Summary[/u][/h2]
There is great potential with Chaos Gate, but if you’re on the fence, I would recommend waiting to see if the developers stop messing with the game first. For some reason they see it as a great priority to mess with the balance of a single player game. My campaign went through the initial balance and two patches. I was lucky that none of the patches hit me too hard because I didn’t even unlock half the classes until after the big nerf. While the campaign can be stalled out or even replayed – I don’t think the game has much replayability unless they address the tedium in replaying the same battles over and over. That said – it was still really fun to play through the game at least once. If you enjoyed XCOM 2, you will likely enjoy this as well, but be aware it’s not just a new coat of paint.

It is with a heavy heart and a righteous fury that I submit this report. The tactical simulations provided to our initiates—codenamed Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters—are not merely flawed; they are an affront to the Emperor’s strategic brilliance. If our Brothers fought as these simulations dictate, the Segmentum Solar would have fallen millennia ago.

1) The Sin of Indolence (Lack of Testing).
The cogitators governing this simulation are plagued by scrapcode. On numerous deployments, the sacred machine spirits have stuttered or failed entirely. To release such a tool without the proper rites of purification and testing is a dereliction of duty that borders on tech-heresy.

2) The Burden of the Unjust (Poor Balancing)
The Emperor grants us the strength to crush our foes, yet these simulations feel tuned by the hand of Tzeentch himself to sow frustration. While our battle-brothers are elite warriors, they often feel fragile, overwhelmed by endless tides of Poxwalkers that possess unnatural resilience. The "critical hit" logic defies the certainty of Imperial Creed. Too often, a Master-Crafted Storm Bolter fails at point-blank range due to unseen "balancing" shackles.

3) The Quagmire of Lethargy (Slowness & Grind)
War is meant to be a swift strike—a spear to the heart of the Archenemy. Instead, this simulation is a slog through thigh-deep filth. Every action takes an eternity. The animations are needlessly prolonged, as if the simulation wishes to mock the urgency of the Bloom’s spread. We are forced to repeat the same skirmishes over and over to scrounge for basic requisition. A Grey Knight should be hunting Greater Daemons, not performing repetitive manual labor for minor upgrades. It is a "grind" that exhausts the soul rather than tempering it.

This simulation is a Trial of Patience rather than a Trial of Skill. Until the Tech-Priests oversee a massive sanctification process to fix the pacing and logic errors, I recommend all Battle-Brothers avoid this training regimen.

The Emperor Protects.

This game is...essentially just like the new X-COM games, but set in the Warhammer 40k universe. You control a squad of 4 Grey Knights, the Imperium of Man's most elite anti-Chaos forces, who wear the same type of power armor as Space Marines (both regular and Terminator type, although theirs generally looks more 'knightly'), but each one of them also has powerful psionic powers. In this game, you have to work with an imperial inquisitor, Vakir, as she tries to stop a ploy from the Plague God of Chaos, Nurgle, to cover 5 planets in 5 types of diseases/mutations to power a "Morbus" of the "Bloom," which will spread the plague across the entire galaxy.

This game is amazingly good, though I have a number of complaints, which I'll go through first. It does get kind of repetitive, as there are only about 6 mission types: Kill (or extract seeds from) 1-4 seedbearers, destroy 1-3 bloom spreaders (big plantlike monster things Nurgle creates that have a lot of HP), destroy a single Bloom Flower within a time limit, and then "Bring Inquisitor Vakir to a certain point on the map and defend her for X number of turns," this is both the Chaos Gate missions the game is named after, where if a planet reaches max infection you have to win the mission to close the gate; if you fail five you fail the campaign, and it's how most of the "story" missions aside from the last go. Compare this to XCOM and XCOM 2, which had basic battle missions, but also defuse bomb missions, protect civilian missions, rescue missions, retrieve item/data and escape, and base assault missions for certain tough aliens. Also, the maps aren't procedurally generated, by the end of the game you'll find yourself fighting in the same cathedral over and over. Now, they weren't procedurally generated for the newCOMs either, but those seemed to have many more maps.

Related to this is that as good as the aesthetics are, they can actually be kind of annoying in battle. All your grey knights look and sound mostly the same, which can sometimes make it hard to distinguish them. There's limited amounts of customization but other than shoulderplates and tabards, all your grey knights are the exact same color. The only reliable way to tell them apart really is from their backpacks, and those are hard to see if you're not zoomed in. I sort of wish they had gone with another space marine chapter, because for those you would be able to modify the coloring of the armor, etc. which would make things a little easier (for instance, in the old XCOM games, I always gave different classes specific color schemes).

My other complaint is on the strategy rather than battle side of things, there's no real sense you have to protect the planets you're fighting on. In XCOM, not only would you lose the campaign if you lost nations/funding regions, but it would also hamper your war effort, because the nations gave you money and/or other kinds of supplies. In this game, however, the various planets you're supposed to defend in the sector don't give you any resources at all, so there's no reason to defend one over another or really keep track of how many you lose aside from your bimonthly report looking worse, and making sure you don't lose more than 4. Most of your resources come from the Grey Knights commander, and thats kind of annoying. Rather than gradually building up the quality of your basic weaponry through research, you're entirely reliant on random drops for guns, swords, etc., which leads to a lot of grinding that feels unnecessary.

Still, I put 87 hours into this game because it's so addictive. They've got the basic gameplay loop of XCOM down pat, *and* they've done an excellent job at conveying the 40k aesthetic as well! Despite being hard to tell apart, your Grey Knights do look very cool, and all the environments look just like the sorts of grim cathedrals, drop pod littered battlefields, and so on you see in the best 40k dioramas Games Workshop has put out. The writing is also pretty good, though they got an actual 40k author to do it so thats not too surprising, but the dialogue and voice acting for the heroes and villains is both fitting and satisfactorily witty. There's also a ton of lore you can get by talking with Vakir and the other characters in between battles during the strategy section of the game, which is both surprisingly attentive to the lore (like the description of the Thorian faction of the Imperium, for instance) and entertaining in its own right. In general, the game just has so much SOVL put into it that it's one of the best licensed things Games Workshop has put out in a while and a very solid XCOM clone in its own right. Despite the lengthy critiques I gave above, those are less important than the solid basic gameplay loop at the center, so I really recommend this game. This is apparently Complex Games' very first project, and I am astonished they did so well! Hope to see more of em...

Cool game... But it has Denuvo... If you don't know - Denuvo grants root-level kernel access to your computer. It's under the operating system. A dangerous compromise of computer safety and hurts performance. No game is worth compromising your PC with Denuvo in order to play it. Refunded on principle. Denuvo is horrid.

The concept is great, the execution needs significant work though. 

The difficulties are almost nonsensical in how punishing it can be. While games like this do tend to be on the more difficult side, the amount of punishment your characters will receive is almost constant, while the amount of damage they can take feels very minimal, which is odd since they're space marines. They feel like they're as squishy as an Imperial Guardsmen. 100 pox walkers wouldn't touch a space marine, let alone a grey knight, yet if you're not careful in the early stages of the game, you can lose a marine to 1 or 2 pox walkers. The other thing that makes the "difficulty" setting feel like it either wasn't tested or simply doesn't work right is the amount of RNG in a map. The enemy seems to be able to call-in endless reinforcements, and the plague marines seem to be able to just heal whenever they want, even on the "easy" difficulty, the RNG can make the experience a slog to get through. If things just don't go your way, you're better off restarting the mission until you get it right or just abandon it all together. The game balance really feels overwhelming at times, where one wrong mistake means you've basically lost the round.

You'll find that your characters are constantly chasing the objective to keep up, and complete the mission before the game spawn too many enemies for even a space marine to defeat. Weapon balances don't make any sense unless it's simply to make the game more difficult and unnecessarily tedious. A trashy cultist auto-rifle of stubber does more damage than a storm-bolter, Plague Marines can just hang out in psychically charged promethium fire and only get a little warm. There are annoying mechanics that allow stationary enemies to just get free, incredibly powerful attacks on your characters with almost no recourse and they're harder to kill than most of the actual enemies. Their range of attack is also probably close to if not double the range of your own characters. The Purgation Marines you can field have a laughably short attack range, making them nearly useless considering how much you have to move characters. The design makes the Grey Knights and Space Marines as a whole feel significantly weaker than the lore, and even other games in the same universe suggest. While I expect X-Com clones to be difficult, it feels like they made this hard in all the wrong ways. It's frustrating. Developers completely ignored lore to make the game more difficult unnecessarily. After the time spent with the game, I can only come to the conclusion that the developers think a Space Marine is just some normal guy with cool looking armor on, because that's what the Knights feel like.

It's not a bad game, but it's also a far from good game and not worth the $40.00 price tag. If you're interested in this game, wait for a sale, a very big sale. It would ironically feel like a much more consistent, and less frustrating experience if you simply changed the Grey Knight characters into Imperial Guard, at least then their lack of starting abilities and generally weak feeling characters would make sense. There's not been a great representation of what a Space Marine is in a video game since the 40k Space Marine game released over a decade ago, and I'd love to play another game where a Space Marine feels like an actual space marine. Your low-level prisoner in Warhammer Darktide is going to feel much more powerful than a Grey Knight in this game. I want to like this game, it's just doesn't do itself any favors. The presentation isn't bad, it looks like a 40k game, they look like Grey Knight Space Marines, except at the end of the day the game doesn't play like you're a Grey Knight, or even just a Space Marine. While the game looks the part, at the end of the day it certainly does not play the part of a Space Marine well at all, and to a frustrating degree.

TLDR: I think the game still needs some optimization work. The framerate on some levels drops as low as 10 from 60 during the enemy turn in particular. I have a suspicion this is Denuvo related. Further, even for minor wounds, the wound recovery time is way too long and needs to be balanced better. I have had some at 40+ days for minor wounds. This means you cannot use the same character and build them up as per the RPG element of the game. The audio in-game is very good, but not outside of it. The story doesn't make much sense lore-wise either. So while the author is, in my opinion, qualified, I am left wondering if it was double-checked by somebody more familiar with the lore? The interactions between the Imperial factions stand out to me as lore-breaking in particular. 

Special mention to the outrageous price for two items, one character and all the twitch loot you can get by watching streamers for hours on end. I think they need a better marketing department, to be honest. Charging people so much for things that should be in the base game is not acceptable. 

Full review:

Do you like X-COM? Do you like 40k? On paper, this should be the game for you. 

Overall the gameplay is good, though wound recovery time needs balancing. 40+ days for minor wounds isn't acceptable. I mention this as even weapons that lore-wise wouldn’t damage Aegis Armour do so regularly. Cultist Autoguns are the main example. This would be forgivable if wound recovery did not take so long.  Some of the abilities that show up at random are either useless or absurdly powerful. Due to being randomized, they often affect mission outcomes greatly. Imagine fighting through a mission that was super hard, only to know you likely have to reload and hope that ability does not spawn again. This is incredibly frustrating. Otherwise, I think the game is very good; though I'm not too fond of cover being up to 100%, I think it should be capped at 80-90%.

Sound-wise, the voices and battle sounds are great. Honestly, they are some of the best I have seen from a 40k game. Outside of battles, minus the voice acting, it is subpar. This takes away from the immersiveness of the setting. I had hoped for better. 

Story-wise, I think several missions come across as filler and do not contribute meaningfully to the story in any way. When you have the Inquisitor, Astropath and other characters written so well, it sucks having to grind through meaningless missions that do not contribute overall. Dawn of War 2 at least had missions that were grindy, but there was a purpose overall to do them. Here it feels like you get a small reward, but that is all. I would like to see that improved. The interactions between the Imperial factions also needs to be improved as well. 

Performance-wise, it can be all over the place. My system is high-end, so getting frame rates as slow as 10 on the enemy's turn is not great and takes away from gameplay. I note this only happens on some maps, whereas others are near perfect 60 across the board. I would hope the developers optimize it some more and hopefully remove Denuvo. 

Finally, one cannot neglect to mention the marketing team deciding to make players watch over 10 twitch streams for items. Who thought that was a great idea? Further, the items + characters in the special edition could have easily been included in the base game. Neither adds anything meaningful to the experience, as far as I can tell.

In conclusion, I would give this game a 7 overall, but it is a 6 due to the crappy marketing and value for DLC proposition. I hope the devs know that this would be a solid game with more optimization. Perhaps market it better next time? Buy it on sale.

EDIT: The Devs were kind enough to give the community the twitch items in an upcoming update. I am bumping my overall score to 6.5/10. It is good to see devs listening to the community. Now please remove Denuvo.

This game starts off mildly, you begin with 4 Grey Knights and each one is a good bit stronger than any individual unit you'll run across. Around the 5 or 10 hour mark you're going to notice a power spike in enemies that, if you're not fully utilizing the game's systems, will destroy you. This is the point where you need to optimize your Knights and their builds - looking for ways to generate bonus AP (Interceptor crits, Justicar abilities, Stun -> Executions)

How long it takes you to figure this out is about how long you're going to be getting beat into the dirt - 10-20 hrs.

If you do figure out your builds, about 30 hrs in is when you should feel the power shift back to your side. Your higher leveled Grey Knights are now power houses, with a few of your roster able to solo entire pods of enemies. And it only gets more nuts from there; the last 15 hrs of this game, when you're giving Chaos Marines wedgies and taking Nurgle's lunch money, are worth all the time you spent dragging a squad of critically injured Knights back to your ship.

I really like this game. I think it does some things to differentiate itself from XCOM 2 that are mostly great, such as removing hit percentages and disincentivizing the turtle playstyle of XCOM (moving up partly and overwatching each and every turn) by adding the chaos meter, among other changes.

But these changes don't always play out like it would seem. For example, they get rid of hit percentages. Great! But what this really does, I've found, is just move the RNG to the critical hit chance. So instead of your turn (and possibly the mission) riding on you hitting the enemy, it rather rides on you getting the critical hit with a 60% chance. Functionally a lot of the times it turns out to be the same as XCOM's punishing hit percentages. 

I think one of the big downsides of the game is the out-of-mission management, it's just not nearly as fun or engaging as building up a base in XCOM 1/2. You upgrade your ship, sure, but it feels like there's no player agency in this. There's just a set amount of upgrades that you follow, with half of them being absolutely critical and half being worthless. (Protip, farm servitors and upgrade your ship as much as possible before the map expands, makes life much easier). 

By far the biggest downside of the game, in my eyes, is the continued reliance on XCOM's old enemy pod system. I HATE this system to the extent that it's ruining the genre for me. Every mission (in every game) boils down to slowly making your way across the map, making sure to pull each enemy pod one at a time, and making sure you're in the exact perfect position before you send the one guy in to aggro a pod. Yes, in this game they give everyone full movement/action points when you spawn a pod (again, great!) but it doesn't change the fact that every mission becomes a game of pod management, where if you draw more than one pod it might as well be mission over. I don't know why so many games rely on this system, it sucks and needs to go. Xenonauts 1 and 2 have shown the old system still works perfectly. Go back to it, or come up with something better. It sucked in XCOM 1 and 2 and it still sucks in every game that copies it.

All that ranting aside I return to my original statement, I really like this game. I've played it for almost 100 hours and I still need to start another game with the Officio Assassinorum content. A turn-based strategy game set in 40k (and based on the Grey Knights no less) is a dream game for me. There's just a few things that keep it from being amazing.

Let me begin by noting I've never been interested in the Warhammer franchise nor universe. I've always recognized a Space Marine, but I've never been as versed in lore as longtime enthusiasts. Nevertheless, I purchased Chaos Gate since I enjoy turn-based strategy games and the cinematic trailers were alluring.

Chaos Gate has essentially whisked me away into a different dimension, and I have no desire to play another game anytime soon. The only problems I've encountered have been small quality-of-life ones, and there were a few technical glitches upon release that, fortunately, I didn't have to endure like the majority of players.

For what this is worth:

I don't typically write reviews, but I genuinely hope you'll give Chaos Gate an opportunity. I believe the pricing of this game to be a steal considering all the experiences it offers.

Some remarks beforehand:

* Game needs a bit of polish. 
* The models and animations look like they are from an older era (which has its charms, for sure. But its nothing like Total Warhammer 3 for example). 
* The weapons and balancing of the armor might need a revision. 

But all in all, a title i'm already quite enjoying. And while not 'as' in depth as an Xcom 2 game 'yet' (so far for me at least), I'm enjoying it. Solid mechanics idea's so far that really seem to work.

I LOVE the fact that i can change minute details about my Knights, down to the voices, armour details, last names ( which are spoken aloud as well as be displayed on the knight on certain places). It really makes me care more about them, instead of 'generic marine nr 5'.

I have played several 40K games who have all tried their own spin on this genre of Xcom like gameplay, from mobile to PC games. And this is the first one where i'm actually enjoying myself.

Each class of knight has their own feel to them and has a varied roster of traits they can unlock in a tree.
(so far, no idea if one Knight can have all of them, but hey.)

It feels like Xcom married Dawn of War 2 in terms of loadout mechanics but expanded heavily on them. Such as the ability to unlock upgrades for your gear. 


I would love to see this kind of game (with perhaps a bigger budget), with other chapters. Could be the same setting for all, with minimal narrative changes or references, so long as the chapters have their own styles or changed options/gameplay. 

Such as Black Templars (Templar visuals with correct colours, no psykers, themed weapons and traits, stratagems etc) compared to Blood angels or even Imperial Fists and so forth (just some founding chapters would be enough in this case, or possibly to create your own generic second founding one). Just roam about the galaxy, doing missions, trying to beat back a warp event/invasion or other xeno races. Leveling up your Marines, building up your base/fleet in a freeplay scenario. Expending resources or requisitioning more from your chapter/the imperium. Collect gear and personalise all of it like in this game. 

Heck, a system/game like this with an expanded roster choice to also play as a strike force of Imperial Guard, Sisters of Battle, etc. I would be amazing to have the choice to play as a different faction for another playthrough. 

Would happily buy the next game in this series if that were the case.
Stopped letting me play it when I went offline. That'll teach me not to check for this Denuvo nonsense. I'll know better next time, but for now? Don't support this anti-consumer trash.

This game is apologetically difficult.

Halfway through the game you have a mission that wants you to defend an npc, who has the best abilities in the game, and is useless while being defended, against hordes of heavily armored enemies and daemons.
This is fine, but these enemies can ignore you and just walk right up to the npc and two shot her without you even getting a chance to defend her.
This is on normal difficulty.
This mission is required for you to see the rest of the game, and the special unlocked classes, such as chaplain, librarian, purifier, and paladin.
Whats more is that these boneheaded developers who don't play their own game, nerfed the best abilities into the ground.
Why? This is a single player game, whats at stake?
Absolutely nothing.
Over the this games life cycle; over watch has become completely useless, and more often than not you will be surrounded by enemies that will tear you to pieces and because these enemies get attacks of opportunity, you can not attack one without being attacked by three others.
At random points your stratagems will become unable to be used, and at other points the grand master will deny you any buffs or points to which you buy gear.

In order to win you cannot experiment or you will fail; you either play the meta or you WILL fail, even on normal difficulty.

Plus, you play as Grey Knights, the best Psykers the Imperium has to offer, and if you want the best gear in the game, you have to NOT use your psyker abilities.

[h1] Better than XCOM [/h1]

First, I confess I am a huge XCOM fan who has played the two latest games extensively on max difficulty. W40K: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters could have easily been called XCOM: Grey Knights and it would have been ok, with one difference: this game is better than XCOM.

Allow me to explain.

1 [b] This game has no RNG [/b]. You read it right. Your genetically mutated space wizard-warriors with millennia of combat experience on their shoulders are easily capable of hitting a large slowly-moving target at 20 meters. There is no roll, they hit, that's it. The catch is that the damage is based on range, buffs-debuffs, etc. (but not on RNG), so you have to play carefully to maximize your impact. However, if you play strategically and know what you are doing, your result is almost guaranteed. In XCOM, you are always betting against your PC.

2 [b] No frustrating base building [/b]. More than building, you are repairing your ship. There are no empty rooms to fill and no RNG that defines if your base will be a powerhouse or a total piece of garbage since the beginning. Even if the base-building experience is slightly reduced compared to XCOM (still, more similar that what other hardcore XCOM fans would admit) this game offers an interactive campaign with exploration, enemy ships chasing you, warpstorms, etc. So, you don't get bored with that. At least after the first part of the game.

3 [b] All classes matter  [/b]. Some classes are better than others at very low level, but as soon as the game starts warming up you discover that all f them are formidable in their own way. Classes, buildings, and game progression are structured in such a way that you are soon able to recruit at a level that allows all classes to be competitive.

4 [b] Enemy variety [/b] There are so many different enemies and so many buffs/debuff you and the AI can cast based on the scenario you are playing and the particular situation you are in, that you are always facing something new.

Strongly recommended.

Great game, but not without its problems. 

-PROS
- Great XCOM-like gameplay
- RPG Character development is great
- Runs really well (at least on my system)
- Great visuals
- Good story (I love 40k but I'm not super well versed lore-wise)
- Fun and interesting maps

-CONS
- Bad UI. It's just too chunky
- Wounds take far too long to heal. Definitely needs balance
- Because of the wounds, you'll find yourself in a position where all of your best soldiers are too hurt for too long. This leads to having to handle tougher fights with weaker solders more often. Instead of swapping out one or two wounded veterans with a couple of fresh recruits, you'll find yourself having to go into tougher fights with a team full of newbies.

Overall, I think this is a really good game that could use a bit of balance to be even better. While I can understand the frustrations others are seeing with this game, I personally think it's positives outweigh the negatives. Especially since the negatives can easily be patched.

Daemonhunters is fun!
It's definitely descended from the hearty stock of XCOM2, with strong influence from Gears of War: Tactics (Itself strong descended heavily from XCOM2), and some Xcom Chimera Squad. Now take that pedigree and place it squarely in the Warhammer 40k universe and that's Chaos Gate Daemonhunters.

Give XCOM2 is probably one of the best and most fun squad tactics games ever devised, so borrowing heavily from its DNA is a perfectly fine thing.

Daemonhunters uses a lot of the same formula, and that's fine. You are a small task force of Grey Knights, a powerful, elite group of Space Marines, themselves already powerful, genetically engineered soldiers of the Emperor. Fresh of a victorious crusade against the daemons of Khorne, an agent of the Inquisition drops in and "requisitions" your battered, limping strike cruiser to chase down an emerging threat from the disease god, Nurgle, known as the Bloom. You take command of the Grey Knights, the ship, and the mission to stop Nurgle's Bloom before trillions of souls are snuffed out in a Chaos-fueled pandemic.

As in Xcom2, you fly your damaged ship (the Baleful Edict) around the map of the known world, splitting between the strategic world map and tactical battles with your soldiers against the ever-growing forces of Chaos. With you is a colorful cast of chatacters. Your second-in-command attoning for past failures Ectar (Bradford), your somewhat inhuman engineer Lunete (Chen), and your resident mad scientist who researches the alien tech for you, Inquisitor Kartha Vakir (Tygan). All superbly voice acted and character-animated I might add, your crew works with you on the twists and turns as the campaign unfolds.

You work on fixing up the Baleful Edict, stamping out new infestations of the Bloom, growing the power of your Knights, finding better gear and equipment, and completing research and mission objectives. Your Grey Knights have a talent tree with moves that grows outwards from the middle almost exactly like Gears Tactics. In battle you have three actions (just like Gears Tactics) instead of Xcom's 2, and if you stun an enemy, you can do a special execution that gives your squad another action point (also exactly like Gears Tactics). When you smite the last enemy in view and drop "out of combat", everyone in your squad also automatically reloads (and gets their action points back), a wonderful quality of life choice wisely borrowed from Xcom Chimera Squad. Unlike those other games, the Grey Knights know neither weakness nor fatigue, and when you get INTO combat, instead of being caught flat-footed with no action points, your whole squad immediately gets all their action points back.  AND they can sense the general location of enemy pods beyond your view with a combination of their auspex scanners and warp sight (which are marked on your map), so instead of tip-toeing around scared or having a stealthed Ranger spot for you, you can charge into battle with purpose. And as such, you can combo dropping out of and back into combat several times in one really long turn. It's even feasible to finish an entire map in one long turn of multiple rounds.

Innovations include a Will Power system, which is essentially a form of Mana Grey Knights use as capable sanctioned psykers. You can spend Will Power on your combat moves which come from a solider's class and talent trees, OR pump it into melee and ranged weapons to give them extra kick which usually includes more damage, and special effects that depend on the weapon, such as armor pierce, armor break, more stun, burning, deleting enemy action points and more. This all comes at a price, as pulling "mana" from the Warp excites the forces of Chaos, pushing Nurgle closer to being able to work blasphemous curses onto the battlefield, buffing Chaos troops or hexing your Space Marines. There's a meter that tracks this, so you can work around it.

Unlike mortal humans, Grey Knights are all proficient in nearly every weapon, so it can be kind of difficult to understand who does what at first. Especially when they have a four-branch talent tree. But Purgators are basically your snipers and grenadiers, using long range guns and grenades. Interceptors are your rangers, dashing (and teleporting) to enemies and chopping them up in melee. Justicars are a mix of heavy melee and tanks who can donate their action points to other squad members for a profit. Apothecaries can wield combat surgery implements that can slice the enemy or heal your troops, as well as buff your guys at range and cast slows and bleeds on the enemy. Purifiers are Purgators who like grenades but then flamethrowers. (They have a melee tree too but meh). In theory Librarians and Chaplains have various spells, but I've never really had a use for one in multiple play-throughs.

You get new weapons and troops from your ultimate HQ on Titan, earning requisition points for missions, and  doing extra credit chores for the Chapter Master like promising not to use any grenades on a mission (budgets being what they are I guess). Win a mission and you'll be a shown a selection if things you could buy with your Requisition Points, OR every 60 days you can put in a good word with your boss to sweeten the pot on the quality of gear that will be shown as a purchase possibility.

Daemonhunters has a similar setback to Gears Tactic on troops, which had a similar "troops show up sometimes" mechanic, which is: Often a new troop will show up who is like level 6, who you've never met but immediately outclasses the level 1 and 2 guys you've had sitting on the back burner in the C team who never see action. Xcom has a special touch at adding character to your troops and nicknames, and the distinct skills of the classes. Lots of people have stories about an amazing scrape one of their guys got into (or died valiantly not getting out of). I can't even remember my Knights' names, it's just "oh my Max level Interceptor is still hurt from that boss).

As with Gears Tactics, Daemonnhunters has bosses and they're pretty cool. One, Munificus, is a lot harder than the others, but they're all pretty interesting. Strong enough to be nervous, but not so hard that you can't get them figured out, probably in one try. 

All told the mix is fun. It's fun powering up knights, finding better gear, seeing the story progress, fixing up the ship, and generally watching everything get more powerful and come together. I recommend it for anyone who likes squad tactics games and/or the 40k universe. It's a AAA entry in the genre and frankly I'm already ready to pay for a sequel.
This used to be my go to game while traveling, on airplanes, etc but now requires you to be online every time you boot it up just to play an entirely single player game

For context, I played this game without any DLC as reviews made me wary, and I believe some of them played a role in lowering the general rating for Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters, which I believe is a shame. Also worth mentioning I started and finished this game in Ruthless (3/4 difficulty mode), using saves, and actually quite a lot of that. I only played the first XCOM (which I loved) so I won't go into an extensive comparison with that franchise.

The story is efficient, I have only partial knowledge about the 40k universe but I do like it and to me it did the job. The little trio of characters are maybe a little cliche but for such a franchise they make sense each in their own right. The same goes for the aesthetics; dark and "dirty" colors, dismemberements with dynamic animations, arsenal of weapons, all in all this blends well with what you'd expect from a 40k game .

The gameplay may seem tedious at first, it took me quite a few hours before understanding how to read the whole HUD or use some of the game mechanics, and honestly it's challenging at times but learning the subtleties after quite a couple unsuccessful attempts (which I tried over and over until I found a way like the savescum I am) felt all the more rewarding, like each turn was a new puzzle to solve.

You gotta like turn-based, of course, but you also gotta like customizing builds and find synergy, which was a plus to me. The game features many classes (8 in the vanilla game, a few more with DLCs), each having different builds, meaning you can have two Marines of the same class but with a different specialization, and even at level 9 (max) they won't have everything in the tree, just to give you an idea of the possibilities. You're only allowed 4 Marines per mission so when picking a hard one you better think carefully about how to balance your group and what you will likely need. I personally like to experiment different tactics so I really enjoyed that part of the game. There also comes equipment: you may (and should) sometimes spend several minutes in the pre-mission screen just browsing and picking equipment, although I agree with some commentors that the interface could be easier and faster to use and read.

Melee fighting is given some love in that game, to the point that you might be in for a struggle if you pick a "mostly ranged" composition. Not only can you melee attack as part of your action move (the Emperor knows how precious action economy is in turn-based games), but a CRIT with a melee weapon allows you to pick a vital part of an enemy for various effects; some of their abilities can be disabled, you might make them bleed etc, all of that on top of dealing extra damage. And here my good people, I must say there is blissful satisfaction in chopping down limbs and be able to "damage control" a powerful enemy that you cannot kill within a single turn.

Missions feature something that gives the game its spice compared to similar games, "Deeds", that is to say optional objectives you may pick upon the start of the mission for better rewards. While sometimes it might be quite straightforward (i.e. "Kill 8 enemies with ranged weapons"), some, usually the ones that lay the greatest rewards, will give you interesting challenges, such as being unable to CRIT for a whole mission or not being able to use Willpower (aka most of your abilities)

RNG does play a part, not in terms of hit/miss (you actually know in advance how much a shot will deal, with variables such as cover reducing it and such) but to another interesting mechanics, "Warp surges". This bar progresses over the course of a mission or when you use abilities, and each time it reaches its maximum, it will trigger a random negative effect (the variety is actually quite wide, this is Chaos-borne after all). RNG also applies to encounters: if you saved before a mission and aren't actually satisfied of your party, load your game, start the same mission again, you will see that you might not meet exactly the same groups of enemies.

As for the enemy variety, it offers a satisfactory array, if memory serves more than the first XCOM plus a few (cool) boss fights although I regret that some foes are met almost only in early game, I wouldn't mind butchering them in larger numbers later on (thankfully, Cultists are here for that). Now I get some people might hate RNG, but I'd take that design over repetitive gameplay, which would be bound to happen otherwise at some point in that type of game.

Every now and then the game will lay a couple of different missions at once, and since you have to move to get there and there is a limited amount of in-game days to complete them, you are never able to do them all (failing them will increase the "Corruption" of a planet, and you don't want a planet to get at max). I gladly admit this part may be flustering as sometimes you are not even able to reach 2 of them, and again I confess I reloaded a couple of times when RNG was really too much in my disfavour. You will also have to manage resources... and they are scarce! Even trying to optimize gains, it was only until LATE in the game I stopped feeling starved for requisition. Which story-wise makes a lot of sense, and I enjoyed that challenge, but if that's not your thing be warned that it's bound to happen.

Those game phases also yield events you can react to, some random, some scripted with a regular schedule (namely, reports). The ones most interested in story lines will appreciate that you get to make decisions and get some different dialogs, however those are purely strategic and do not change anything to the plot, and as a usual a fan of "taking sub-obtimal decisions because it fits the character I'm playing or the story I want to tell", I sadly had to push away that tendency of mine because of my priorities of the moment :) But anyway, that's part of playing a "strategy" game over a choice-based RPG so I easily got over it.

If I had one single harder criticism, it would be about something that I learned about just before I played the final mission, which btw I still did not use for reasons that will become obvious; you aren't in fact the most rewarded when like me you try your hardest to keep every single Marine alive till the bitter end (I hate losing party members... Darkest Dungeon was a life lesson to me, but when I have other alternatives, I can't stand seeing any of them die... ahem... but I digress). Well, it turns out with the right upgrade, losing some of your Marines rewards you extra ability points for a living one, the only way actually if you want to have a Marine maxed out. Very sad :'( but yeah, grim-dark after all. As I said, you can beat the game without using this once, so feel free not to do so. The positive counterpart being, if you don't voluntarily send Marines to their deaths but it happens by accident, you're not losing everything... Happy? :'P plus throwing Marines on purpose to their death around the end of missions is probably too risky a strategy in hardest difficulty, but I just got annoyed knowing it's actually the thing to do to get the best min-max.

Aaaaall in all before I rant about even more aspects of the game, let's TLDR: I had an amazing time playing and finishing that game and beating the many challenges it kept tossing at me like a WAAAAGH! tosses Gretchins, I seem to understand that this is a small studio so kudos, it's likely I'll play the game again in a few years, but I'll get some of the DLCs that time, and this is all a big LIKE on my part :)

I recommend it if you're into that kind of "XCOM-like"/turn-based and generally a 40k fan (but the latter is not even needed imo) and overall feel ready for the challenge, see aforementioned elements. Just in case, start with the base game only if you're not sure you'll like it, but really, it has a soul and the devs deserve some love for it.

The game is really fun and what bugs I have encountered have been mostly UI bugs that you can easily fix with a bit of menu switching. The gameplay itself is pretty much XCOM, and I'd say that unlike Hired Gun actually holds up better to its proverbial template than that game did to Doom.

The game is fun and can be downright punishing too, as the AI isn't slow to adapt and isolate misplaced units. Several times was a battle brother ever so slightly out of position only to be met with an onslaught of fire. 

And that's fun. The game encourages tactical, thoughtful gameplay, and isn't just bolter-porn (which might be a negative if that's what you're after).


I even had this cool little situation where 1 of my Knights was downed, so I pushed the other 3 forward to help, only for a warp occurrence to spawn an army of pox monsters. The 3 were subsequently overrun, only for the first guy to stand back up and with the Emperor's light in his eyes completely clutch the day and get all my guys back home.

Moments like that are Warhammer as fuck and that the game gave me one of those 2 hours in? Fuck yes, I'm all for it.

I should love Chaos Gate and I'm ploughing on with it until something else grabs my attention, but I can't honestly recommend it.

Imagine if XCOM and Rogue Trader had a baby that got the worst bits of both - that's Chaos Gate. 

Never have I missed XCOM's random number generator more, and that difference is supposedly one of the good things about the game. And it's actually more annoying than that because there are plenty of random events that can be much more crippling and annoying than failing a 95% chance roll - including at least one that can take a whole squad out of action for a good amount of time. Playing on Normal is hard enough, so how anyone manages on higher levels is beyond me and, if like me, you're time-poor and prone to save scumming there are a very limited number of save slots. And there are games that manage to be different from XCOM whilst doing things a lot better than Chaos Gate - Jagged Alliance 3 and Phoenix Point for two.

And neither is it particularly good as a Warhammer game. There is a plot as such but, unlike Rogue Trader (etc), it basically serves just to ferry you from one battle to another, although the cut scenes are very pretty. There are 4X's that have better plots. And the battles are very samey, with a limited variety of enemies and not much more variety of objectives. There are also various timing mechanisms in battles and the strategic layers that funnel you towards certain points and ways of playing. And although there should be plenty of room for experimentation, the high costs of getting things wrong discourage it.

I'll admit that the Grey Knights and Nurgle aren't my favourite bits of 40K lore (which, until Rogue Trader, is very poorly explained for those new to 40K) but my first impression was that I was in for some sort of space marine power fantasy, which I'd happily buy into. However, the difficulty spikes are all over the place, and although there's a difficulty indicator for each mission I found one 'extreme' boss battle relatively easy but another 'extreme' spore collecting mission absolutely impossible. I accept that a hard tactics game shouldn't hold your hand too much, but Chaos Gate actively hides useful information.

At least I'm running a fairly powerful PC so I haven't had any of the bugs others have reported, but there are things that don't make sense - including one particularly annoying issue with line of sight. 

I'll update this review if my impressions change but I can't think of a tactics game that has made me more desperate for an XCOM3.

I like this game way more than I expected to. It's basically X-COM with a 40K skin, but I find it more enjoyable. The missions are resolved quicker, but still feel action packed. It works pretty well on Steam Deck. I can only think of one part that requires using the touchscreen. The rest can be navigated with the Deck's controls.

The core gameplay is solid, but some of the design decisions are baffling. I have no idea why the game forces you to completely enable or disable things like ship warp-travel cutscenes in the options menu instead of simply letting players skip them with a mouse click when they don't want to watch them.

Another issue is movement. There is no reason the game couldn't let you press Tab to switch control to another soldier while one is moving. Instead, you're forced to sit there and watch a single unit slowly walk all the way to its destination before you can continue issuing orders.

The result is a painfully slow pace. Unfortunately, the lack of mission variety only makes this worse. You'll be replaying the same mission types over and over again, and before long the game becomes extremely repetitive and tedious.

Because of that, I strongly recommend that first-time players start on Easy or Normal difficulty. On higher difficulties, the game is not only harder but also far more time-consuming. Since story progression is tied to research, and research takes longer when you're struggling through tougher missions, the overall campaign can start to feel like a slog.

I can easily see players burning out and dropping the game halfway through. That's exactly what happened to me.

After some 180 ingame days I think I have pretty good picture what the game offers, even if I havent seen all the enemies yet its safe to say I overpaid for this experience.

At a guess, I am about 75% finished with the campaign, so it's time to give this a review. If you are either a fan of turn based strategy games like X-Com, or the greater Warhammer 40k Universe, there's a good chance you're going to like parts of this game. To truly love it, you're probably going to need to be fans of both. 

Chaos Gate improves upon some of X-Com's annoyances, and then abruptly adds several grating annoyances of it's own. One of the biggest complaints (at least of mine) with X-Com is the notorious 90% chance missed shots. Chaos Gate does away with that for the most part, and shows the damage you will inflict with each attack. There is a still a chance to miss certain ranged attacks if the enemy is behind full cover, or other unusual circumstances. Knowing if your enemy has an automatic chance to block a melee attack is something you the player have to factor into each turn's plan. I like the cover system, and later in the game there are weapons and skill that will help you damage enemies hiding in partial cover. The game also shines in environmental damage. There is an abundance of things that explode, or crash, or topple over onto the enemy. This is essential in the early game, and players that learn to use the environmental mechanics will have a much more enjoyable time. And then that enjoyment will be tempered by the RNG rogue-like events. My fully leveled apothecary was given a random quest to attain the paladin special class... and was killed. No combat, No decisions to be made beyond sending him on the quest,  just a notification that he's gone. That hurt. I'm still bitter. The warp surges can also throw a wrench in your best laid plans. There are a few, like the witch one (damage to your marines for using their psyker abilities) that can be just brutal when you're under the gun.

Speaking of bitter, there's a lot of hate for the DLC. I enjoy it for what it is, but agree it made the game much more difficult. I did not purchase the DLC until I had my first Reaper down, and felt comfortable with the feel and tactics of the game. You can really feel the difference once those technophage missions kick in. My advice is the same as many others, do not enable the DLC until you are sure that you are ready for the challenge. 

The difficulty overall is sloped. The early game is the hardest, especially if you aren't carefully planning. Injuries take a long time to heal until you build the appropriate facilities in your ship, and there are always other things you'll want to build first. It's easy to find yourself sending wounded marines into battle because you have exhausted your ranks. Something to consider though, later in the game, dead marines = extra ability points via the commune function. If you want to fully skill up a marine, it's going with to be with the blood of his brothers that fell before him. Mid game was most enjoyable for me. As you begin to get the skills that make a difference, some upgrade weapons and armor, and some support facilities built on your ship, there's more room for experimentation and riskier tactics. You will want to level all your marines as there will be times that events or injuries may put your "favorites" out of play for some time. You will want kitted out and skilled marines by the time you are tackling the Reapers. 

Warhammer 40k fans will enjoy the overall storyline, callbacks and lore. The voice acting is pretty good, and most characters are good examples of the universe. Except Kai...  some of his decisions do not fit the char or the story, and are just chuff to make trouble for the player. Overall, if you are a fan of the Grey Knights, you'll feel satisfied they were treated with the respect they deserve. If you've never heard of the Grey Knights before, this is good introduction to a very secretive group of psyker space marines. 

I'm giving the game a thumbs up, and fully intend to finish it. I can see myself revisiting it again for a challenge with the higher difficulties or new DLC.

Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters isn't perfect but it's fun and has a ton of heart and atmosphere.  It can get aggravating to wait for the computer to make all of its moves, most notably at the end of the game when it has 20-25 units on the board, tactical play at that point can become tedious and repetitive. But overall the game is engaging, immersive and, as I mentioned above, fun.  If you're a fan of the X-Com reboots and Warhammer 40K in general than this game is for you.  The art direction is great, the lore is on point and the campaign is interesting and full of twists and turns that do the writers a lot of credit.  I should mention that the designers opted out of the frustrating RNG combat model used in X-Com.  Every action's outcome is predetermined and you can see what that outcome will be before selecting the action you want, no more missing at point blank range, hallelujah.  The game has a lot of re-playability and I can see myself playing through it a second time.  A solid 8 out of 10, have fun, stay alert and keep your boltgun handy.

Just finished the game on Legendary. First play through on Regular was super fun, and I learned a lot. In the 2nd play through at Ruthless, it was pretty dang hard but I somehow squeaked through. I discovered the trick of standing on the bloom warp and sometimes being able to stop a reinforcement squad from appearing. I learned which weapons and armor were worth spending precious requisition on, and I avoided certain builds for abilities that I didn't use very often. I got to try a few of the harder classes to recruit: Chaplain, Librarian, Paladin. 

At the end of game 2, I read some online guides and realized I had been missing out on some other tactics, like making Interceptors into melee machines instead of primarily using them for fire support as I had done originally. I learned about how to really double down on certain knights' strengths and rely on passive equipment and auto abilities much more, instead of active abilities that suck up WP and limited supply items like grenades.

This is one of the hardest slog games I've ever reluctantly enjoyed.

"X-COM WITH WARHAMMER 40K GREY KNIGHTS"

That's it, that's the game. You should be interested, it sounds awesome. X-com like map, x-com like base, x-com like squad, mechanics, turns, even an x-com like abrupt ending.

However, this game (especially if you tick on the special addon enemies) is damn near impossible for poorly designed reasons. If you're playing on hard, you will lose. Period.

The game mechanic that separates this from X-com is a corruption/peril timer at the top of the screen that increases every turn no matter what from 0-100%. It raises 10-20% just on turn end, and then increases by amounts any time your characters use psychic abilities, which they pretty much have to use to do any decent damage, or heal, or move to the endpoint on time.  Bottom line: you're gonna hit 100% multiple times in a mission. 

When the bar hits 100%, portals open, enemies get double health, armor, your guys die, bad stuff happens, missions fail. You barely survive a lot of missions.  "Well that's normal!" you think. Yes, it would be, but the game is balanced in such a way that when you fail, the game gets harder, and you have limited knights to use, so your 20 hour run quickly becomes an unwinnable situation where you have to restart. There is no possible way to reclaim your win on a some 50 hour campaign.

That wouldn't be so bad if you didn't HAVE TO COMPLETE a 5 hour tutorial on every run.

This game was fun. The detail is cool, the lore is cool, and the moment to moment play is great, but there is no skirmish mode or quick way to get to that fun. It's bordered and locked behind a slog of story, ui, brokenly difficult mechanics that are designed to waste your time. 

In my 143 hours of playing this game, probably 120 of it was spent frustrated and pissed.

If you're a 40k goon and really wanna see some power armor space marines smash things, you will like this game, but be prepared to meditate on the 10 hour setback you got when your Grey Knight in terminator armor just died to one cultist with a 9mm or you stood on a burning corner of a building, because in Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters, your space marines are made of cardboard, apparently, and using an apothecary to heal is an immaterium-ripping effort.

This game would be improved 100-fold if bracing armor, using a narcethium, and area attacks with weapons didn't FOR SOME REASON, require psychic power. I don't know why it does, but it does. "WAVE YOUR FLAMETHROWER FROM SIDE TO SIDE!" "okay" "well, now that you've done that, you've screwed the fabric of reality and now all the enemies are bosses, gg."

First 8-10 hours were kinda rough but get through that and the game takes off. With my current setup (on standard diff) I can teleport the squad in and wipe the entire room in a single turn.
