An exercise in tedium, designed by someone who doesn't quite understand the setting.

To start this review, I'm a long time X-Com player and enjoyed the original Chaos Gate back in the day.  I'm also a massive WH40K fan (since 1991), and this is not the game 40K fans have been waiting for, despite ADB's story and some really good voice-acting (though the barksets can get repetitive).

The mechanics are vaguely similar to X-Com, with you having specialists that have different abilities and access to different weapons, abilities and wargear.  However, the mechanics surrounding the abilities aren't really explained, and their usefulness is debatable (blind, for example, seems to do nothing other than a pretty light show - it doesn't affect the enemy's aim or cancel their overwatch).  Firing a weapon is heavily influenced by your line of sight, as you'd expect, but the range is terrible.  Further, your weapons, whilst accurate purifying death-dealers in lore, are no more effective than the weapons being shot at you.  In fact, the heavy stubber and autogun, which you should shrug off, do a considerable amount of damage, making them better options than your own weapons.  A strange idea, because in lore the autogun is essentially a caseless assault rifle (think the Aliens Pulse Rifle), whilst the storm bolter fires 0.75" rocket-propelled/stabilised rounds that penetrate the target and explode violently inside the target, their steel and silver tearing apart the target and embedding them with purified shards of metal, which are anathema to Chaos spawn and their followers.

The 'seeds' you have to destroy/harvest (it's the research mechanic) in 90% of the missions go from being randomised enemies to being Nurgle Feculent Gnarlmaws, and acquire a bullet-sponginess along with an armour regen and an AoE regen for all allies nearby at the end of every turn.  If you jump in one of your Interceptors, hoping to get some decent melee damage, then the AoE of the Gnarlmaw really injures your Knight.  You encounter Death Guard fairly early on, which can be an interesting miniboss during these early missions, but also become dreary with their constant self-heals and firepower that rivals the cultists super-autogun.  I've yet to progress to later missions, but so far nothing's compelling me to do so.

Your ship/base of operations, the Baleful Edict, needs repairs/upgrades, which is a nice base-building mechanic, apart from the constant Interventions that you have to do, which will lead to you having to rebuild your upgrades, or having increased research times because one of the crew has a sudden sad on because they didn't like your decision and turned into a child about it.

The game does a very poor job of selling the idea of commanding a Grey Knight team, the Emperor of Mankind's super-secret psychic super Marines that should cut through cultists like they're not there, and should only be mildly worried by Chaos Marines.  These guys are daemon hunters, and are the best that the Imperium can muster (short of Custodes, but they are to Grey Knights as Grey Knights are to regular Astartes - double-plus hard buggers), taking on the greatest threats in the galaxy and cutting them apart with ease.  I understand that there's a separation between game and fiction, and the game needs to provide a challenge, but there's a difference between a challenge (which is something WOTC did well) and sheer boredom/misery.  If the cultists are corrupted Guardsmen/PDF, then you are a Loyalist Guardsman cos-playing as a Grey Knight. I'm sure after 30+ missions my Marines may be useful, but I'm not sure I want to subject myself to 30+ missions of this to see it. 

The game doesn't so much have a difficulty gradient as a series of difficulty cliffs that make what could be interesting encounters into something of a grind.  You can almost see the enemy AI algorithms in action, which makes them predictable yet a chore.  Great stock was put into this destructible/explosive terrain that litters the maps, but the enemy will never be anywhere near it, and if you want to shoot a statue to knock it onto a group of enemies (say) then it will never allow you to do it.  I've double-checked I was in range, had ammo, etc, but the game decided I couldn't do it.  

TL;DR - It has some interesting mechanics and ideas, looks great and has the right atmosphere, but is let down by poor explanations, terrible weapons, and boring missions and enemies.

Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters has a lot going for it, but it has far more going against it. As something of an XCOM connoisseur, I wouldn't recommend playing this game. But lets have a look at it in detail, starting with the good things,

+ Excellent combat flow. Upon encountering enemies, assuming you aren't already in combat, all of your Knights will immediately gain full AP (action points). This means you won't need to worry about triggering an enemy group with your last guy, thus removing the need to carefully tip-toe forward and speeding up missions. Upon killing the last active enemy, your Knights will once again immediately gain full AP, meaning you can go right back to running across the map at breakneck speeds. The regular missions are definitely the strength of this game.

+ Engaging boss fights. A rarity in NuCOM style games. There are several bosses in this game, and while one or two are a bit finicky and annoying (looking at you Plague Hulk) most of them are genuinely engaging, and require different approaches to defeat.

+ Class variety. All classes are at the very least viable, although some don't stack up very well, like the Purifier, while some are basically auto-takes, like Purgators, Justicars and Paladins. Likewise, each class feels distinct and will have a different effect on the battlefield.

And now for the negatives... The... Many negatives...

- Random events. Random events kill this game hard. In other XCOM games, random events are only ever triggered by player action, be it progressing the story or choosing to engage with said event at all. In Chaos Gate, random events are thrust upon you, and almost all of them are some form of choice between suffer from a catastrophic event, or suffer slightly (and I mean slightly) less by sacrificing a large amount of valuable resources, putting you in a constant downwards spiral where accomplishing even the most simple tasks becomes a slog as random events constantly attempt to disrupt your efforts.

- Certain missions destroy the flow of combat, namely Noctilith Crown missions. In these missions, enemies do not spawn normally, instead arriving in an unending stream via reinforcement portals. The problem with this is that the game will always consider you in combat, thus preventing you from gaining full AP after a fight and slowing the pace of the game to an agonising crawl as you attempt to make forward progress through an unending stream of enemies. These reinforcements show up on EVERY. SINGLE. TURN by the way, so no breathers. At all.

- Some of the DLCs drastically throw the difficulty out of whack. So you want a Dreadnought, do you? Cool, well here's a mission where you meet the Dreadnought but don't get to keep him. Then there's a mission later on where you actually get the Dreadnought permanently, but don't let him get too damaged, otherwise you'll be scalped of valuable resources to repair him, which also puts him out of action for a while. Then there's a mission where you get a second ship, which allows you to perform two tasks at once. Oh, but you don't actually get the ship yet, and when you eventually do, it's not that good, as it's too slow to respond to missions, and the missions it actually can reach will just get your guys wounded, possibly out of action for a loooooong time. Also said missions are left at the mercy of autoresolve, and anyone with any experience in XCOM games with autoresolve, like Xenonauts, knows that anything that isn't a 100% chance is practically guaranteed to fail catastrophically.

- The end of the game is incredibly tedious. After a certain story event, the end-game is triggered, most of which is an unending tide of missions, giving your guys absolutely no chance to recover meaningfully between them. Assuming you make it through that, you then have to get through not one, but two boss fights in quick succession. You better hope you have a thick roster of max level Knights, and you better hope none of them are out of action.

- Overall the game is too punishing. Are you doing well? Stop wasting Chapter resources, oh and serve a penance as well that will leave your best Knights unavailable for a long time. Oh, and while that's happening a Morbus Gate mission showed up, but you don't have enough active Knights to do it, and not enough time and Servitors to prepare an Exterminatus. The game literally punishes you for doing well, and seeks to drag you down into the pits of misery at every opportunity, robbing the player of any agency at all times.

I guess the wait continues for a good 40k XCOM game. C'mon GW, you have Deathwatch vs Tyranids, literally the PERFECT recepie for an XCOM style game.

I have probably written very few Steam reviews, but this time I decided to go for it.

I started and restarted this game about three times. It humbled me so hard that I eventually switched to Easy. And Emperor help me, it is still very good.

Positives:

1. The writing is excellent. I do not remember playing a turn based game with writing this strong. Characters feel believable, interesting, and accurate to the lore. Their interactions make sense. I am genuinely glad I stopped and came back two years later, after learning much more about the Warhammer world and especially the Grey Knights.

2. The premise is fantastic. You are an uncorruptible psyker Space Marine facing Nurgle’s filth against all odds. It never stops feeling appropriate or heavy.

3. Combat, when it works, is extremely satisfying. It feels brutal and impactful. Classes and abilities are lore accurate, and the precision system is great for controlling the battlefield.

4. No percentage based hit chances. No save scumming. No losing a mission because the dice decided to hate you.

5. I never played XCOM, but from what I have seen, the Warp Surge system feels better. Same core idea, much better execution. Random effects are manageable at first and only become dangerous if you play inefficiently, which adds pressure without feeling unfair.

6. Enemy variety is better than people claim. With DLCs, I kept seeing new units introduced at a steady pace.

Negatives:

1. The game becomes repetitive quickly. Missions boil down to three or four objective types, and maps start to feel identical. I could probably navigate them blindfolded now.

2. Most classes, especially advanced ones, feel weak or pointless. I used Purgator with psilencer constantly because other weapons are clearly inferior. Interceptor is mandatory because one WP or AP attack deals as much or more damage than a grenade. Justiciar is essential for AP buffs and masculine urge to tank for your brothers. Purifiers, Chaplains, and Techmarines were very disappointing. Librarians and Paladins are strong but often come with awkward or suboptimal builds.

3. High level Knights arriving with pre allocated stats is baffling. I genuinely do not understand who thought this would be fun.

4. The ship feels fragile even when fully upgraded. It still gets damaged too easily, disabling critical systems and punishing you outside of combat.

5. Outside combat, movement is painfully slow. You should be able to move the whole squad at once. Missions drag because of this. Positioning is also too strict. How you first trigger enemies often decides the entire fight, forcing pixel perfect scouting to ensure full AP and squad proximity.

6. Very low level missions become a chore. An auto resolve option with some cost in wounds or resources would save a lot of time.

Conclusion:

Despite its flaws, Chaos Gate is one of the most immersive and lore faithful Warhammer 40k strategy games I have played. It can be frustrating, unbalanced, and repetitive, but the atmosphere, writing, and core combat loop carry it hard. If you like Grey Knights and can tolerate some rough edges, it is absolutely worth your time.

The characterization of the 40K universe is very well-executed and is certainly one of the biggest differentiators for those who are looking for something similar to X-Com, without actually being X-Com again.

The game favors more aggressive tactics and heavily penalizes players who want to play it safe (which leads me to believe that this is why the community oversells the game's difficulty). A series of dynamic systems are in place to discourage you from standing still and being subtle and careful in your offensive. 

Unlike its counterpart, Chaos Gate doesn't abuse percentages and RNG to the point of frustration, making each attack happen more or less as planned.

Frankly, this feeling of control is quite refreshing. I've never felt the need to restart an encounter because the game penalized me for something I didn't do. And I don't think I've ever felt the frustration of missing an attack that seemed guaranteed.

It's the pure satisfaction of seeing mechanics working consistently. The rules are clear, the difficulty is sharp, but it simply works. As long as you understand how the dynamics work, it's not hard to make the right decisions.

But the magic kind of wears off once you discover that there's almost no variety in the missions you choose, aside from the story content, which is usually locked behind research that requires a good deal of repetition.

The content basically stagnates in the first few hours of the game and soon after, the experimentation with the few customization options you have available either runs out or funnels you towards the best tactics to deal with all the threats in the game.

Unless you deliberately decide to improvise or suffer the misfortune of accumulating penalties, you're unlikely to be surprised by anything the game throws at you.

I started out playing on normal, and with minimal guidance from players who warned me that the game shouldn't be played like X-Com, i don't think I ever had to tactically reorient myself to what the game was throwing at me. Honestly, in 20 hours I didn't even come close to losing a single character other than to a random map event.

As good as it is, I never felt the pressure.

Perhaps the game gets better on higher difficulties or with the DLCs, but from the tone of the conversations, i think it's simply another case of being more efficient at the same tactics used on lower difficulties.

The game does a good job of developing an addictive progression loop, balanced with combat missions, but it fails to retain the same freshness as games like X-Com.

But it is what it is. At least the game has enough personality to be more than just a clone.

Yes and No. [hr] Daemonhunters is a great isometric X-Com-style game, but it suffers from a measure of Darkest Dungeon Syndrome, heaped upon a failure to properly represent the characters you are portraying.[hr] Daemonhunters has many wonderful systems in place to engage you, including of course its excellent tactical combat, refitting of your cruiser, and research of The Blight plus the beneficent abilities that will help you fight it. It uses an Action point system of very tiny scope i.e. 3 pts. per unit to divide amongst movement, interactions, attacks, and special abilities. The totality adds up to make a very good game.[hr] BUT... [hr] ... The game hammers you. The Warp Surge mechanic - a timer that bestows all sorts of negatives upon a player, from plagues to weakenings to reinforcements - is an omnipresent tiring thing that always has you under the gun... rushing from A to B to C. As such, a player does not have much luxury to employ certain stratagems, like luring enemies into an area full of destroyable architecture. You have to bull-charge forward, and the more effectively you do that, the better. Some researches, some cruiser technologies can help. Still though, you never get a break, and the aforementioned bull-rushing is almost [b]always[/b] your best option. That aspect plays into the main gripe with Daemonhunters. [hr] You aren't playing Grey Knights.[hr] As an appreciator of the lore we are immersed in either from dabbling in tabletop days or from playing the MULTITUDE of Warhammer 40k games out there, many of which are quite good, you understand the place Grey Knights have in the Empire Of Man: Grey Knights are the most potent cloned stock of engineered warriors, the most dedicated, augmented by their super-human psychic abilities. They are the demon-hunting special forces from amongst the special forces of the Space Marines of the entirety of The Imperium. [i]And yet[/i]... in Daemonhunters you are no better than a regular Space Marine with a couple of interesting psyker traits. In 40k lore, Lasguns and Stubbers (conventional ballistic weapons) are at the low end of the tech pole. Plasmas, Meltas and Bolters (gyrojet round weapons) are at the high end. From the very beginning of the game, you are confronted by hopeless human Cultists with primitive Stubbers. You should wipe the floor with them. [b]And yet you cannot.[/b] These Cultists will out-range you, pin you, lay low your psychic shields, strip your vaunted elite armour, and tear you a new one. While playing you will fear the appearance of run-of-the-mill Chaos units, nevermind anything like a plague priest, a vehicle, or a buffier demon. You play in constant terror and dread of such.[hr] Compromises were made to make a (good) challenging game that works. And it works very well. But the compromise always rubs you the wrong lore way: these are trusted Marines who have occasional superior tech and interesting powers, not at all the Grey Knights of 40k lore. And that reality constantly gnaws at you, especially as entirely conventional Chaos enemies pound you into the earth. One who knows more than I about 40k lore put it this way: a single Grey Knight wouldn't be challenged by 3 to 4 Cultists and their Stub-guns... he'd be sweating against 500 Cultists. 500. Daemonhunters always feels off because of that.[hr] I played up to point X on Normal. The combination of that lore scope and the unrelentingly brutal treatment of those aforementioned mechanics made me quite decisive about abandoning my Normal Campaign in favour of starting a new Easy one, whatever such a setting may bring. Just not interested in [i]suffering[/i] so much, Darkest Dungeon-style.[hr] Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters is still a great game, just not quite what it should have been.

This one's tricky to review and leaves me conflicted. Essentially whether it's for you is down to your experience in RTS games and how you like your difficulty served. Ultimately, for most non-RTS genre gamers, it's a pass or deep sale at best.

WHAT'S GOOD:
- The story is actually pretty decent - predictable but with its fair share of interesting characters and storied Warhammer lore. I'm not a Warhammer guy, but I enjoy a dark imperium as much as the next guy - and this thing delivers.
- The voice acting is really good. It left me wanting the ship-board personalities as battlefield regulars to spend more time with them.
- Artwork is nice - thematically it's W40K to my untrained eye, but uses really vibrant colours in interesting ways. It's not D3 unicorn mode, but we get urgent purples and vile greens in all the right ways.
- Controls, whether M+K or controller, are tight and intuitive. I think a lot of RTS games, esp. with console controls, could learn from this.

SO, ABOUT THE BAD:
- The game is absurdly difficult, but not because (IMO) it's "hard." Instead, it's cheap.
 a) While it has difficulty settings, those mostly impact battlefield conditions, but where it gets oppressive is the world map. You're constantly juggling resources you just don't have enough of, in a situation where you're always backsliding due to the chaos invasion conditions. I think "easy" should relax the anxiety-inducing elements of overworld management, but it doesn't feel like it does.
 b) When you're in a game, you might size and equip your squad for the intelligence the mission screen gives - but then the game will warp in reinforcements at the end to pressure you, sometimes with units you've never seen, using abilities you've not had. While this can be fun, when overlaid with the stretch goals that can penalise your overworld Requisition points, which you don't have enough of, it feels like stretch wins/losses are random rather than down to any strategic prowess.

Overall, this game is well-built, but for a more hardcore crowd. I can't speak to whether that's computer RTS fans or Warhammer fans, but as a more casual RTS enjoyer this was a DNF due to absurdity leading to frustration. Easy should, in fact, be easy. I ain't proud, but if I pick that option, then honour the choice.

Feels like Imperial Guard Simulator, except you're cosplaying as Grey Knights.

Did you know regular bolters do more damage than storm bolters?
Did you know that human cultists are more durable than space marines?
Did you know that Chaos Marine armor is far superior to what Grey Knights wear?

If you enjoy watching the finest of the Astartes hit a regular human with a force halberd and repeatedly fail to kill him, this is the game for you.

It's actually not a terrible tactics game, aside from the clunky UI and slow animations and transitions, but it manages to make the Grey Knights feel grossly incompetent at every turn. Power armored marine took a punch from a one-armed cultist? Wounded for thirty days. Cultist crouching behind a box? Essentially invulnerable to ranged attack. Every mission type requires you to push push push relentlessly, so you spend most of your AP trying to catch up to enemies who spawn in by the half dozen, then fall back into cover to shoot you to pieces. Because yes, human cultists are better marksmen than Grey Knights, their rusty stubbers outranging even your purgators.

Hence Imperial Guard simulator. Were I running a dozen lasgun monkeys, I'd understand how digging gribbly cultists out of their cover could be a rough fight. Instead, I'm watching terminators get punched and take damage.

The ideas in it are interesting, but this is a game where their only ideas for challenges are to put a timer on every mission and reward you for bringing fewer soldiers. As a result, every fight plays out the same: rush forwards at full speed, because the enemy gets more actions than you and is almost guaranteed to use several of them to fall back, drawing out every fight so the bloom can spawn in more of them or buff them to insane levels. The devs response to this was to nerf the mobile classes.

This game is criminally underplayed. Not underrated - most reviews for it seem positive - but just not played by enough people. How do I know? Most of the achievements I got for exceedingly easy story progress and character leveling are under 10% of player base. Mind you, that's not because I'm good - it means people just stop playing early on and that sucks.

Yes, WH40k is a dedicated but niche fanbase - but this is a rare combination of a solid gameplay model and a story that doesn't necessarily require the player to be a hardcore lore nerd to enjoy.

Gameplay: Have you played X-COM 2? Did you like it? This is Gothic far-future X-COM 2. That is the best way to describe it. And because of the 40k license, it actually makes sense why plasma weapons and railguns are wielded side-by-side with swords and (war)hammers. Turn-based grid-style movement and action with partial and full cover mechanics. Gone are the percentage-based hit chances from X-COM - the game just tells you if you are going to hit the enemy or not. No more 94% to-hit shots missing five times in a row. It makes up for that removal with enemies that start out strong and do nothing but keep getting tougher.

Graphics: It's not aiming for any graphic awards and it doesn't need to - it's character models and proportions are fantastically true to their tabletop model roots. Your squad and the main characters get particularly well-done details and facial expressions that convey their thoughts and feelings quite well, with Ectar and Vakir being the standouts. One small quibble I have was the weird decision to have many enemy models just fall apart into a heap of limbs and organs upon death - it fits the grimdark setting, but it just felt like a toddler tearing apart the limbs on an action figure.

Sound: The soundtrack for this game a gem. The music for the various scenes and the battle map bgm are quite good, but the standout is the gothic-cathedral choir music from the loading screens and ship hub. It is haunting and beautiful.

Replay: This will be determined by your affection for the core gameplay loop. If you're the kind of person (like me) who has sunk hundreds of hours into multiple X-COM campaigns, you'll likely do the same here. The story is quite good but doesn't really demand multiple trips - so this will come down to your how much you like the core gameplay and the license.

Overall, if you cannot tell, I love this game. Even if you're not a WH40k fan, it is a very well done turn-based tactical RPG that is worth the time of any fan of the genre. I hope that a sequel would be in the future for it, but given the apparently lower numbers of players based on the global achievments, I won't hold my breath.

tl;dr This isn't a bad game and the presentation is lovely but the game was clearly made by people who LIKED XCOM Enemy Unknown without really getting it on a fundamental level and is immensely frustrating as a result. Buy it on sale.

I really wanted to like this game, man. I'm a pretty zealous XCOM fan and I've been into Warhammer since I was old enough to call people bad names on my computer. Some people hear the words "There's a deritative pastiche of XCOM Enemy Unknown on the store with a 40k skin" and sigh in disappointment, I heard about it and bought it on sale immediately.

Now, let me describe this game to you: In a modern XCOM format, you play as a faction of undersupplied, undersupported and overworked soldiers who have to face down dangerous hordes with little in the way of supplies, abilities or care for your life. Enemies will wreck your shit early on and shrug off many of your mightiest attacks, brushing off your most determined strike like it was a fly hitting a whale's back. 

"OP, is this an Imperial Guard game?" you may ask. Some of you might ask "OP, is this a Deathwatch game?"

No, you play as the Grey Knights. Grab a hold of that bewilderment and let me walk you through the review.

If your 40k knowledge is surface level you might not understand the disconnect here. In the fluff the Grey Knights are often regarded as 'Mary Sues'. They're all psykers, their aegis armor is obscenely powerful, they are immune to the corruption of Chaos, they have unique weapons that are better than everyone else's, access to special armor (The beloathed Dreadknight among them) and they're considered the strongest of the Astartes. Modern lore has cut this down, but this is just the facts.

...Anyway, in this game your starting Storm Bolter is less dangerous than the patchwork junk guns wielded by the cultists you fight as trash mobs.

This is just a microcosm of this game's weird and frankly frustrating balance. The soldiers you command are clad in fanciful armor wielding divine weapons but for my entire 20hr campaign I just felt... weak? The Knights take obscene amounts of damage which can be unavoidable if RNG does not favour you and swamps you with enemies, while they dish out middling attacks in kind. Sometimes you do get lucky, and the opportunity to get multi kills appears. You get consecutive executes which grant an extra action point or 9 enemies stand near a pitfall in range of someone's knockback grenade, or your overwatches actually kill something. 

But these are rare, the bulk of combat is spent in a brutal slog where oftentimes you're better off sheepishly avoiding enemy patrols and gunning for the objective. Problem is, this impacts your XP gain, so the game can and will frequently outpace you. Wound timers are OBSCENE, sitting at around a month, and you don't get near-endless cheap reserves like in XCOM. Oftentimes the only solution is to repeatedly deploy knights which, sadly, just compounds their wounds further unless you roll an easy mission. The cycle of hurting in this game is insane and it actually puts many of XCOM 2's more challenging reworks to shame on that front. 

More than anything, it feels as though much of this game was made by someone who hated a lot of the usual strategies in both modern XCOM titles. Overwatch has been gimped for the player and is no longer a particularly safe option for units in difficult movement situations, grenades have knockback to prevent consecutive throws clearing a huge group, distant healing is a rarity and the lack of accuracy buffs from high ground means that risking a high-ground-low-cover position just isn't worth it over a low-ground-full-cover position. This is a game that puts you in the boots of the Imperium's own demigods and demands you play it like a poorly balanced XCOM 2 overhaul.

Ultimately, what made me quit was the Warp Surge mechanic. There's a meter in each mission which confers a random enemy buff or player debuff when it hits 100%, and is increased by turn timers and using Willpower (WP) moves. I get the intent; encourage players to move swiftly without a hard timer (as in XCOM 2) and to punish people spamming their psyker attacks willy nilly. Unfortunately the end result is an already punishing game becomes outright spiteful. Your psyker attacks are limited by WP something fierce, and in the early game they're often vital to stopping you getting turned into putty by the enemy. 

Many of these issues are *alleviated* later on but not entirely absent. In truth, it's rare for me to review games without finishing them, but Daemonhunters is such a mess that I felt compelled to just quit and review it now. I enjoyed the opening hours, and Robyn Addision's voice as Inquisitor Vakir filling my ears again while FFXIV's MSQ is suspended for the time being, but I can't keep going. The potential this game has and the rare moments where it seems like a competently made game arguably make it MORE frustrating than if it was simply mediocre on its own.

This is the best XCOM-alike since XCOM 1/2 itself, for me. It's got all the core pieces, plus a variety of clever innovations: huge boss fights, more conversations and characterization for key NPCs (provided you can enjoy 40K-style cheese!), gorgeous/hideous and interactive environments, more expansive and versatile gear options, some major conveinces to make map-crawling less of a chore, and more. There's a lot to like here.

And yet, it still felt like something was missing, in the end.

So, here's a list of nitpicks:
* Perhaps the biggest one: if you're going to pick a single 40K faction to make an entire lengthy campaign around, Nurgle is... well, his key mechanical themes are A) dudes being aggravatingly hard to kill, and B) tossing out aggravating debuffs like candy. This kind of thing makes for a great sometimes food, but when it's the only course on the menu, it doesn't take long for it to get tedious.
* Knight skill progression was designed to be very breadth focused, rather than depth, like XCOM. This made it somewhat less satisfying for me; there aren't really many super cool skills that feel hugely rewarding for your guy to have achieved. Instead, a lot of the really cool stuff is shunted off into mastercrafted wargear.
* There's a wide range of gear, but for weapons and armor, each piece you receive is unique, rather than something that can be provided to everyone. This means you need a whole *lot* of it to outfit your squad, or else need to pass stuff around and re-equip everyone at the start of every mission.
* Furthermore, the upgrade options you receive are randomly selected when missions come. With the large pool, it's quite possible that you will *never* manage to obtain the top tier versions of some weapons or wargear. I ran a pretty protracted campaign (~800 days), and still ended up with some annoying gaps.
* Oh, you also hit the level cap on your Knights pretty soon, if you get around to building the XP upgrades. This again contributes to their individual advancement feeling unsatisfying.
* The class balance felt pretty off. My Justicars seemed to reign supreme of the base classes, and of the advanced options, the key ones seemed to be Paladins (who are more or less specialized Justicars) and Chaplains (because they provide some great buffs for Justicars). Everyone else could contribute, but none felt quite as ubiqitously important.
* Oh yeah. There are advanced classes which unlock halfway through the game, but outside of a single random event I encountered, you don't promote people in to them; you have to recruit them as newbies. Hope you have room in the barracks.
* The fact that you only ever get a party size of four really limits your options for bringing more exotic or niche support classes.
* You have a finite resource for adding localized strategy+tactical buffs to the map, Prognosticars. However, partway through the game, the map also doubles in size. I hope you didn't spend them all too early.
* There is a certain mechanic which is *very* useful, and a majority of the tech tree is dedicated to it. It also is permanently disabled once you begin the end game missions. That was kind of annoying, given that I stalled for some time to finish off the upgrades for it.
* There is a certain very hyped character which, near the end of the game, you get to take command of. He has some decent party-wide buffs, but otherwise seemed intensely lackluster compared to, say, my Justicars. It was a little disappointing after all the build-up that he needed to be coddled like an escort quest rather than being an unparalleled badass.

That said:
* GREAT, incredibly tense final mission, XCOM 3 take note.
* The gearing options are fun to play with, much more so than the base XCOM games offered.
* Psychic powers are awesome. It'll be hard to go back to any cousins where everyone has so few and limited active abilities.
* The story actually threw a few twists that surprised me, and was enjoyable.
* It's 40K.

A DLC seems to have just been teased, and I'm looking forward to that. :) 40K could absolutely get a ton out of more games in this genre!

So, nearly 100 hours of game play and I've completed the campaign for the first time. Could I have done it sooner? Yes, you can complete this in 50 hours or less if you want to rush, but I wanted as complete an experience as possible. 25 hours or so were spent on an easy campaign to learn the ropes and make mistakes.

The good - Do you like XCOM? Are you a fan of 40K? Then you'll love this. I like the fact that you don't have percentage chances to hit, it's automatic because the characters are supposed to be some of the best warriors in the universe. The AP system is great, especially how with careful management you can keep a 'turn' going for a very long time, and the buffs you apply to characters that may only last one or two turns can last the whole mission. The amount of customisation and the amount of effort that was put into the game design is wonderful. I really enjoyed this campaign.

The bad - The major turn off for me is just the pacing of progression. The hardest challenge is the early game when you have no ship upgrades, no skills/powers, and no good weaponry. Once you get halfway into the campaign you start to snowball and it becomes less and less of a challenge. Most of the bosses can be defeated in one turn even when you're playing sloppy. If this game had given you some skills to assign at the start of the campaign, and some items to start making some actual team builds, then the early game would have been a lot more fun and less grindy. You only feel like you're actually able to play the game fully once you're half way through the campaign. This is a shame, from the achievement stats/percentages it's clear that most people give up well before the real fun kicks in. I wish the progression and difficulty had felt more even, or was flipped/scaled better.

Overall I love this game, I may come back to purchase some of the DLC's if they go on sale. After that, I may try a play through on the highest difficulty. I think the re-playability of this is slightly hampered by just how repetitive the missions are. Maybe some of the elements unlocked by DLC will ease that feeling.

I want to stress that Chaosgate is still leagues above the average 40K game that usually releases on Steam. The IP has a pretty big history of receiving games that are little more than shovelware, or attempts at strategy that are no deeper than a puddle. Chaosgate is not that, you can tell the Developers actually tried and to varying amounts of success, even managed to make a decent video game. The problem is, it has barely any long-term viability, is poorly balanced, and insists on certain mechanical trends that really badly need to die.

The biggest issue is balancing. If you are a tactics veteran, and tend to plan out your turns, really think about your choices and usually default to playing stuff like this on the hardest difficulty, then the game very rapidly becomes way too easy. There is an initial adjustment period, particularly if you try to apply any previous experience from other games like X-Com. But once you figure out how the little cogs and pieces all fit together, the game devolves into obvious solutions to the same recurring problems.

Bosses and Elites are deleted in a single turn with the right setup. Once you know what you're doing, and your squad progressively gets more abilities, there is basically nothing in the game providing a real challenge. Enemies are frequently just erased the turn they appear, and if they are not, there are so many way to turn them into non-threads. Campaign upgrades increasingly take the edge off as well. It has the same issue as Mechanicus did, where there is basically a reverse difficulty curve, that does not even start that high either.

If you are a newcomer on the other hand, or simply approach this kind of game more casually, then you'll have the exact opposite problem. The design is very focused around a "Do bad, keep doing bad, do good, keep doing good" approach. Doing fewer missions means less resources, which means less upgrades, which means less power. Meanwhile the game keeps escalating, and it takes almost 5-10 hours before you can usually reach a certain point in the story where your options expand and a threatened campaign could be stabilized.

In that way, the game becomes hard to recommend to... mostly anyone. Newbies will struggle until they figure it out, at which point the game's too easy so why bother? Veterans will have a few hours of fun before they get how the game works, at which point you are basically "done" barring a few dozen hours of bowling over heretics.


The game is also buggy. Damage and range indicators are frequently wrong or don't work. Optional objectives will fail for reasons you were not informed are a factor. Savegames break, making the games equivalent of Ironman basically unplayable.
The developers patches for both rebalancing and other adjustments will also potentially make some of your builds unviable, or maybe you just want to try something else after a patch. But the games internal respeccing is incredibly tedious and stupid to play around (It involves suiciding your knights).

Finally, and this might be more of a personal taste, the game has RNG-Bullsh*t in the form of Random Events. I don't know how many more games need to do this before we can collectively decide that arbitrary rewards/punishments based on fake choices is a dumb thing to have in your videogame, but Chaosgate certainly has them. Pick one of 3 options what you do not have enough context to know on what they'll actually do. Whoopsie, looks like we locked your Arsenal for 60 days.

Seriously, just stop doing this forever.

I really tried loving this game and don't get me wrong, it's not trerrible. It is just that the mix of different game mechanics makes you tired with it before you end the playthrough... What made stop playing it?

1. Very bad character class balance. You have classes that are must have and classes that you may completely ignore.

2. Character experience cap at level 9 which you can get quite quickly and then the game dosn't really reward you for playing it.

3. Having your Knights at level 9 and some equipment of tier III you may find yourself still quite early in the playthrough and not having anything to play for. No unique loot to get, no more exp to grind, just the same repetitive mission all over again.

4. Encounter mechanics where uncovering enemies resets action point of your units so you would preferably always uncover them with your last unit still having AP. Problem is that how and when you do or do not uncover enemies seems really random. One time you will spot them through a solid wall with no windows, the other time you will not.

There are some good ideas behind this title but all in all I have played plenty of better turn-based games, not to mention the Mechanicus, which is also in the WH40k setting.

Too many people compare this game to XCOM. It is FAR more akin to Gears Tactics and makes me realize that not everyone plays as many tactical/strategy RPG games as I do. It's an amazing genre - go play some more games than just XCOM. HMU if you need recommendations. Overall I have been enjoying the game. I like the art, the music, the ability to literally disarm your enemies, and once you get the first healing upgrade and to around level 3 things really start to open up.

The first part of the game IS pretty rough on you (I had some salty words on stream about it NGL). If you just push through that and stop thinking of this game like "Hide in cover" XCOM it really grows on you. There's a lot fun to be had here. I think so far Teleport Strike is my favorite ability. Man that one is just awesome fun to use. The only mechanic that irks me still (at least as of writing this) is that when you Overwatch you step OUT of cover. I got shot a lot needlessly figuring out when Overwatch is (and is NOT) helpful. 

Final note: You don't have to kill everything. In fact you RARELY have to kill everything. Focus on your objectives and then GTFO. I know that's a different mindset than some of you are used to in this type of game and it's a bit of switch. Once you make that change though... it's fun times ahead!

Tl;dr: A solid game that rivals some of the best WH40k games that have come out in recent memory. A must-buy if you like WH40k and tactical turn based strategy games.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]

- Graphics. The game is beautiful and the art design is great.
- Audio. All the audio is great and really fits the 40k universe.
- Gameplay. A good mix between XCOM and Mechanicus. You get the guaranteed damage of Mechanicus but also the tactical cover use of XCOM.
- Content. A single playthrough took me 41 hours, so there's a lot here.
- Boss battles. The boss battles are really well done, with a small number of unique foes that require different tactics to destroy. 
- Story. What's this, a well-written 40k story with interesting characters and excellent voice acting? Not since the days of Space Marine have I felt such a connection to individual characters in a 40k game.

[b]THE BAD[/b]

NOTE: none of these are game breakers, but they could be improved.
- Progression. The progression of CG:D is limited compared to similar games. You start off with the ability to deploy a 4 man squad, and unlike in XCOM or Mechanicus you never get to deploy more than 4. You also start out with essentially every kind of weapon available, so while you progress and unlock better and different versions of the same weapons, you never really get any "new" weapons with different effects. As the game progresses you unlock some new passive and active gear, but it's not a lot. The main progression comes in the form of leveling up your Knights and giving them new active and passive abilities.
- Available resources. You use a number of different resources that are handed to you kind of randomly based on random mission rewards. A consequence of this is that it's possible to not get enough of a certain resource. For example, you use servitors to upgrade your ship and gain access to certain options and I had the problem where I was not receiving enough servitors to upgrade my ship. You also have to spend servitors to repair your ship as it take unavoidable damage throughout the playthrough, further limiting your resources. This might be an intentional design decisions to simulate the resource-starved situation that the Grey Knights find themselves in, but in terms of gameplay it feels wrong to finish a 40h game with several ship upgrades unfinished. I never even got to try out the Exterminatus! 

[b]THE MEH[/b]

- Character customization. While you can customize your Knights to a decent degree and have everyone look fairly unique, the main differentiation come from what weapons and armour the Knight in question is using. Master crafted weapons and armour all have their individual unique details but you will be equipping your Knights based on stats, not looks, so all you're really left with is picking some details for the shoulders and shins.
- The length is both a good and a bad thing. The limited progression makes it so that a lot of missions end up feeling similar. You can change up your squad and use different synergies for new and interesting results, but I found that I quickly figured out an OP squad that could tackle anything. The only times I didn't use them was when they were hurt/unavailable or the current mission seemed like it would be relatively easy and so I could safely send some weaker Knights to get them some XP.

Its a brutal version of XCOM 2 set in the 40K Universe....but you already know that is you're here! Recommended despite a few annoyances, all detailed below to assist new players:

1. Don't rush to research the next 'objective' in the story. You need to upgrade your marine squad as much as possible to survive and the game seems to take this as a milestone to place harder mobs in the levels.
2. After you research the first objective you have access to strategems...very useful but if the button is 'greyed out' it means your inquisitor Vakir is wounded....try to keep her safe!
3. Speaking of which, have at least 2 teams due to the long wounded recovery time. Can be shortened by upgrading your ship but not until later in the game....it's genuinely annoying not being able to use upgraded marines due to them being wounded.
4. Good initial squad makeup for early to mid game is Justicar in Terminator Armour using PSiCannon (free up on the right middle in their tech tree) and aid the chapter ability from middle bottom. Interceptor using Teleport strike and team fire - all the left side of their ability tech tree. He can also silence casters. Purgator also with a PSiCannon - could be swapped for a second Justicar as he can't use Terminator Armour. Apothecary is your healer so free up right side and right top of their tech tree. Put them in Terminator armour as well.
5. Save often in mission and on the ship....there are random very annoying events which you can to a certain extent mitigate by reloading (warp storms, etc)
6. Prioritise your warp drive...you can't make all 3 bloom missions when they spawn but maybe 2. A cheeky reload prior to the event will reposition the bloom spawns if required.
7. AI uses overwatch and timed grenades a lot so you need to be a little aggressive. Stun is your friend for executions but you will find this hard to do in the early game. Your team is detected at 15 squares and aegis shield will carry over when your team is detected, so shield up just prior to detection.
8. You only get 6 prognosticars so place them with care on the map!
9. Standard difficulty is brutally hard! Missions can last up to an hour as well so its a very long game.

If the random ship events were taken out and recovery time for your marines was reduced it would be 5/5. As it is, 4/5. Recommended.

Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters has a solid foundation. The combat system is well designed and the atmosphere fits the setting well. While the game is initially enjoyable, the campaign becomes increasingly tedious and repetitive over time.

The biggest problem is the lack of variety. The game turns into a grind, particularly with the constantly recurring missions against the Bloom. On top of that, you face the same enemies on the same maps again and again. Once you find a strategy that works, you can apply it to many situations. I also find the tactical variety too limited. The different units' abilities simply do not offer nearly as many options as they do in XCOM 2, for example. This takes away much of the tactical appeal.

Another weakness is the trial-and-error design. Sometimes, you only discover what you are actually supposed to do once you are already in the middle of a mission. This encourages save scumming rather than careful planning, especially when it comes to revealing the map and enemy pods. Combined with the repetitive missions, enemies and maps, the game becomes increasingly tedious towards the end. At one point, I just wanted to get it over with.

There is also a technical issue that was apparently never fixed: the game occasionally freezes in the middle of combat, forcing a reload, which is mildly infuriating. As for the DLCs, they feel artificially integrated rather than naturally incorporated into the game.

Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters is not a bad game. The foundation is solid, and the first few hours are genuinely enjoyable. However, I found the campaign became increasingly tedious because of the grind, repetition, trial-and-error mechanics, and limited tactical variety. Eventually, it starts to feel more like checking off tasks than actually playing a game.

I played another game (Warhammer 40,000: Mechanicus) and finished it after about 43 hours. Although I am not a fan of the Warhammer 40K setting, I found Mechanicus to be a good game worth playing and finishing.

On the contrary, I do not recommend buying Chaos Gate – Daemonhunters mainly because of the combat. The choice to have a maximum of 4 Grey Knights per mission leads to unnecessary difficulty and frustration. The enemies are either few and not very dangerous (making the combat boring) or much more numerous (compensated by a general inferiority in combat), leading to battles with 15 or 20 enemies. At this point, instead of being bored by the easeness, you have to fight against frustration because the combat becomes a search for the correct tactics to avoid too much damage to our four Knights.

The story is ordinary, nothing exceptional, just a simple pretext for the battles. The graphics are nice, with a dark gothic style, as it should be in this setting. It does its job; after all, exceptional graphics are not required for a turn-based game.

The character development part involves the skill tree, there are several choices, and I must say it is well done. The only reason I left the game after just 15 hours is that I did not enjoy the combat.

Be careful, I am a fan of turn-based combat, I have played many starting from UFO: Enemy Unknown (1994), I am not a newbie... then, this is my judgment, maybe you will like it.

As far as I am concerned, I am moving on to something else

BAD BALANCING!!!!

This game has probably got the worst balancing issues I've ever seen in a game of it's class (turn based squad combat).

The game features heavy impact rng elements both in combat and in campaign, which can and potentially will ruin your day. You can literally lose an entire campaign worth days of gaming to rng factors. 

The same accounts for battles. When I first started this game I played on normal, was progressing fine, until one mission the game randomly started throwing plague marines by the droves at me, not just some, but like 12 at a time + cultists and a mage. The game also features a "chaos boon" meter which regularly fills up every turn to give the enemy some nice buffs every few turns, or outright call new ones. There is a great deal of effects this can cause and some are simply absurdly out of balance. Take armour for instance, which comes in points before hp. A terminator armour in this game gives 2 armour. A regular chaos plague marine gets 3 (wtf), then a chaos boon happens which gives every enemy unit +5 additional armour for 3 turns, which means you will have a super hard time doing any damage at all as even chaos cultists get tank like armour. Or your ranged weapons fail for several turns. Or your entire squad gets infected with damage over time effects. You get the picture. This happens every few rounds in a game which has matches that may really take time, like 1+ hour. Since these effects are all heavily randomized a well running campaign can turn into a nightmare out of nowhere. You have no influence on it.

The atmosphere, the equip, the leveling, and especially the destructible battlefield are all nice - like being able to shoot a statue and determine where it falls, preferrably on the enemy, that's new and nice. The game also features research and tabletop known elements like stratagems, as well as upgrading your starship. So in essence, this is a really good game with several new features and probably the worst balancing I've ever seen.

Barely recommendet because of being a good game which gets heavily dragged down by ridiculous rng difficulty spikes and VERY BAD BALANCING!

Short credentials background on me to allow quick judgement whether my opinion is worth it's grain of salt:
-I have sunk hundreds of hours into the moderns XCOM 1, XCOM 2 (modded and unmodded), and recently Phoenix Point (on Epic). I have finished most of those in the difficulty under the hardest mode. Except Xcom 2 which I loved so much that I ended up finishing 5 times at least, including one legendary ironman run.

No spoiler parts:
Length-wise/completion wise:
-The game is long because missions are long. My only run lasted 90 hours, on Ruthless difficulty (Diff 3 out of 4). No Ironmade mode (called "Grandmaster mode" here) which is a good thing because I had to save scum a few times (Under 10 times for the run) because of unwritten/unexplained rules that I had to figure out. I have accomplished I would say over 80% of research and available construction and had a roster of 15 knights, 11-12 which were very oftenly used, and none or exceptionnally.

-Difficulty wise:
If you are an experienced XCOM players, the main difficulty will come from a lot of unexplained rules.
A few examples:
1) Your units have 3 action points. When not engaged in combat, this is also the case, however as soon as combat is engaged by "engaging" a pod of enemy in combat by bringing them into view, your units go back to 3 AP, and after you have exhausted all your AP, the enemy plays. This should be explained somewhere, and it is not.
2) The mission rewards (grimoires, servitors,requisition) are not well explained either and if you are unlucky enough to not understand fast enough that having a lot of servitors will tremendously help your campaign, you are in for a tough readjustment during the early/mid campaign.
3) Some interactions between skills are never explained either. For example if an enemy is suppressing one of your unit and your unit is forced to moved by another enemy, then suppression is triggered. The game is full of these kind of things.
4) The surgical unit building gives knights that only activate when Knights suffer a critical wound after it is built. It is not retroactive (although the text kind of indicates it is. And it should be?!). Same for "Commune with the fallen".

-Bug wise:
The game is relatively bug-wise, except for the quite present "There is something on the ground that should be interactable with, and I can't and I need to reload the quick save to be able to.
The exception is that last mission, which has 2 bugs (one visual, one gameplay) which are not game-breaking but quite annoying.

-Characters customization.
This for me is one of the great strength of the games: Like in XCOM, you can customize your knights and truly make them special. They each have a personal passive and can gain new one either by special events (quite rare) or "Dying" during a mission when you have the surgical unit building.
You will also assign them items (which can be swapped between knights) to accomodate certain builds. Those items are one of the highlights of the customization system, and you can make some truly powerful combinations.
Each class can also be built in different ways, within certain limits. Which brings to my next point.

-Game balance:
The game is not very well balanced as of now. Certain classes/Builds are useless where some others are extremely powerful. It takes a while to understand this. Having an apothecary in every team quickly becomes mandatory.
As of today, I am still looking for a utility to the Chaplains, but maybe I just didn't build them right.
Tips for beginners: Love your interceptors, and build a purgator with a long range Psylancer. 

-Story:
The story is great and the W40K lore is a great backstory for the game. The interactions between characters is great and every named enemy is interesting. The story missions are extremely well done (although at least one early is very poorly balanced) and will keep you interested until the end of this Grey Knights campaign.
Truly one of the highlights of the game and this was extremely well done.

I can't help but compare every game in this genre to XCom, which is a masterpiece and among my all-time favorites. Chaos Gate isn't quite as tightly designed or well-balanced as an XCom, but it's a good time in it's own right and well worth playing. 

It's biggest weakness is that there's not much mission or map variety, which leads to a long middle section of the campaign that feels like it drags. In between revealing events that push the story forward is a lot of doing the same few missions on the same maps, over and over and over again. I got really tired of taking out seed carriers and detroying bloomspawn, but that's all there was to do while I finished key research and levelled up my knights. Adding to the feeling of things dragging on is that your knights become quite powerful in the mid-to-late game, while the challenge level of the enemies tapers off. Standard missions become not only repetitive but too easy. I eventually reached a point where I stopped rotating through my roster, and just took my best knights with the best gear on every mission, because there was no reason not to. They could handle everything the missions threw at them, and they rarely got injured.

Unlike XCom, the campaign here doesn't really push you forward with any sense of urgency. The planetary infestation levels are supposed to do that, but I never really worried about it, just always did the missions on the planets with the highest infestation, and it was never a problem. Apparently there is a special mission type that happens when a planet "Blooms", but I never saw it. Which means you can pretty much just chill out and max all the research and construction, and take your time progressing the plot. 

This game is at it's best in the key story missions and boss fights. They feature unique challenges and interesting twists on the mechanics, and often involve scenarios that are much more exciting and intense than standard missions. They did a much better job of pushing me to play carefully and tactically, using my squad's powers as efficiently as possible, and there were many moments where I felt like I was right on the brink of being completely overwhelmed just before I achieved victory. The final boss fight is cool and satisfyingly epic. I just really wish the overall campaign had integrated some of these tricks into the routine missions in order to add more challenge and variety throughout.

I have a variety of minor UI/interface gripes - like the fact that the star map doesn't zoom out far enough to see the whole thing at once. Missions show a little bar that gives a vague indication of how much time remains before they expire, and they show you how much of the bar will deplete if you make a particular move, instead of just showing you a counter that literally just tells you the actual numbers in days. Similarly, the game doesn't show you how many days each route between planets takes to travel. The only way to know is to watch time tick over as you move, and try to remember. There's other issues like these, places where the game is a bit obtuse with info that should be clearly offered, and clunky in accessing certain menus or managing certain mechanics. But these are just irritants, not deal breakers.

Highly recommend, and I hope to see more 40K games in this genre!

This game is a great thematic entry in the 40k universe and makes you feel like you are protecting a galaxy against an ever growing foe. However on the technical side the game falls on its face.

The UI is very bad and explains very little to you. Some examples being: 
Enemy actions like suppression which just tells you that you will take damage upon doing an action. However, despite consuming action points, things like using your aegis shield or reloading do not trigger suppression damage. Something that is only learned through trial and error (reloading a save). 
Cover destruction is not communicated at all so some times you can destroy your own cover with a grenade or fail to destroy enemy cover with one. Additionally, when moving to locations your Grey Knight can destroy the very cover he is moving to hide behind leaving them completely exposed.
The detection system is just a crap-shoot as there is no way to know for sure how close an enemy can be to you to see you. The only way I have found to work around this is sending a terminator unit to run into the fog and trigger them as he can run back and take hits.
The inventory system is general is an extremely clustered and unorganized mess. 

The Bloom system is a cool idea in concept, but fails in execution. It seems to grow slightly too quickly. Main complaint though is the fact the bloom increases significantly whenever you use any of your abilities. An extremely stupid design choice as it incentives players to avoid using abilities to increase the precious little time they have in missions. 

Thematically, Grey Knights come off as extremely weak and incompetent in gameplay. For some reason, the Grey Knights who are supposed to be the greatest Space Marines in the entire Imperium struggle killing homeless people with cobbled together guns and rusty metal clubs that can pierce terminator armor. As a long time 40k fan and chaos player this is pretty immersion breaking and frustrating. Nurgle can make cultists slightly tougher and stronger but the level of boons that Nurgle would have to give to these cultists to get them to this level would turn them into chaos spawn. It is even worse when you compare with darktide where prison convicts are miles stronger than Grey Knights.

One pro at least is the galactic map mode as it is simple, rewarding, and well explained while being a little repetitive. I often found myself wishing the game was focused on the galactic map and ship management instead of the turn based gameplay.

Overall as someone who is a experienced veteran of the turn based strategy genre and a 40k fan this game had potential but fails to deliver. I would not recommend playing this game. Instead I would recommend Gear Tactics or the Xcom games.

Probably my favorite of all the Firaxis-XCOM imitators out there, and I would say I played most of them.

Despise the obvious similitudes the game does a fairly good job at leveraging the IP it is based on and make sure the differences in "flavor" compared to XCOM are clearly felt, with your Grey Knights playing aggressively, with far less concern for their safety and being fare more capable of taking hits and tanking enemies blows.              

What's best, the illusion of controlling far more powerful characters than your average XCOM soldier is successfully sold while still maintaining a more than respectable level of challenge across the board, from start to finish.

Of course, after a while the player will get familiar with the appropriate synergies between classes, with the most powerful talents, with what equipment to prioritize and said challenge may start to become a bit more formulaic and predictable, but that's true for pretty much any game in the genre and one could make the argument that this is exactly how it's supposed to be ("If I do everything right I can reliably achieve success" is not a flaw, as far as I'm concerned).

If I have to point the game's weakest points, on the other hand, I'd identify mostly two problems.

- first, the laser focus on daemons of  Nurgle as the only enemy faction inevitably leads to a vague sense of repetition by the end of the campaign, as enemies after a while start feeling a bit same-y. 

- second, all the DLCs past the initial release have been fairly underwhelming, not adding much and being arguiably way too expensive for what they offered and added to the formula.

It should probably also be stressed that the game didn't really offer much post-release support past these overpriced DLCs.

I don't even know what the studio is up to these days, but I'll say that an hypothetical sequel with a bit more polish and some added variety (i.e. encountering chaos demons of different factions rather than just one) would have me fairly hyped.

The game itself tries to be a X-COM rip off with not even a close match to the delightful work that the X-COM remaster had. 
 
While X-COM has a fast-paced campaign where mistakes can be really punishing, this game skips all that and even if you make good decisions and you manage to keep everything straight for some time, it will still kick your nuts, because screw you. 
 

The game fancies an artificially created difficulty with the “ warp surge” mechanic, which can basically hinder you every few turns, or buff the enemy every few turns, this is on top of the fact that all enemies usually have much more range than you, they are also  more than you, and practically all enemies have one or more special skills (which can combo with the mentioned buffs or debuffs) 

The game campaign also aims to bother you at every step, for example:

[h1]“Only in Death Does Duty End.” — A Chaplain’s Benediction for Daemonhunters[/h1]

[b]Verdict:[/b] [i]Anointed. Brutal. Glorious.[/i] This is a tactics game that demands discipline, and rewards aggressiveness and mastery with many operatic moments of triumph.

[h2]To the faint-hearted reviewers[/h2]
I hear your laments—this campaign is hard as adamantium nails. You will miscount damage. You will meet new horrors whose tricks you only truly learn mid-fight. You will get spotted by patrols because there’s no tidy detection ring (my biggest gripe), and the best scout—[b]the Callidus Assassin[/b]—is DLC. And yes, you will save-scum. I did. I recommend it. [b]Save at the start of every turn, after every objective, and on the starmap.[/b] Call it the Litany of Precaution. The Emperor understands.

[h2]When it clicks[/h2]
This is not a “wipe every foe” game. Most missions are [b]surgical raids[/b]: strike the node, cripple the linchpin, extract. Doesn't matter if you are surrounded by dozens of enemies - in most maps, the moment you destroy the final objective, you've won.
Early on you’ll feel outgunned; later your [b]Grey Knights and Assassins[/b] blossom into a divine orchestra of combos. You’ll learn which powers and tools each mission hungers for, and you’ll start deleting patrols the instant they appear. The tension never dies—enemies always feel dangerous—[i]but your toolbox outgrows your fear.[/i] [u]Prioritize objectives.[/u] Fight only the fights that matter.

[h2]Playstyle that carried my crusade[/h2]
Unlock a [b]Librarian[/b] as your first advanced Knight and take [b]Gate of Infinity[/b]. [i]One AP[/i] to reposition the entire kill-team, followed by [b]Vortex of Doom[/b] or an execute chain, turns “we’re surrounded” into “we are the surrounders.” Most Knights excel in melee; many foes are nastier at range—[b]so steal the distance[/b]. Still, I had plenty of other tools as well - my Vindicare shined from afar on many maps . My Callidus single-handedly destroyed entire enemy squads before returning into the shadows. 

[h2]Theme & spectacle[/h2]
The story feels straight out of the Ecclesiarchy—valor, sacrifice, galaxy-wide rot. [b]Voice acting[/b] is excellent; the script knows its 40K catechisms without drowning in them. Levels are gloriously [i]Nurgle-y[/i]: cathedrals and imperial sites entombed in biomass, meat, teeth, eyes, tongues and tumors; then you’re boarding plague-ships for good measure. And the [b]crit dismemberments[/b]? The first, and hundredth, time you [u]literally remove[/u] the limb/head/organ tied to an enemy’s ability, you’ll cackle.

[h2]Counter-arguments addressed (and smitten)[/h2]

“It’s too hard.” → It’s [b]demanding[/b]. But every unfairness has a tool: [b]Aegis[/b], [b]Honor the Chapter[/b], [b]stuns → executes[/b], [b]environmental kills[/b], [b]teleport / Gate of Infinity[/b], [b]AoEs[/b]. Learn the litanies; reap the miracles.

“I hate patrols.” → Same. Play tighter: inch edges, hide, run away, bring stealth when you can. Avoid, reposition, fight only when you are at an advantage. It’s tense [i]by design[/i]. But don't worry, there are also plenty of moments where you'll decimate dozens of enemies one after another.

“RNG ruins runs.” → Build around [b]guarantees[/b] (Hammerhand, Astral Aim, Shriek/Vortex, grenades, ledge-throws). The less you roll, the more you win.

[h2]Final Rite[/h2]
Very very recommended. Install. Save often. [b]Gate. Strike. Extract.[/b]
[i]Only in Death does Duty end.[/i]

Good if you like XCOM, or like Warhammer 40k. Must-play if you like both! This game scratched the XCOM-like itch in a way that Gears: Tactics just did not do it for me.

The fights are much more fair than XCOM because they replaced the random-chance-to-hit with damage reduction from cover and distance. The missions are also nicely paced and reward aggressively moving through the maps because they reset your actions whenever you encounter enemies and reset again when you kill them all. Your knights have regenerating shields that take a lot of punishment so I often didn't run a healer at all.  And they have tons of ways to boost their damage in a pinch to finish enemies off. My end game teams with the advanced classes unlocked felt ridiculously strong in a good way and yet I felt every character I had was useful in its own way.

The strategic layer is basically the board game Pandemic but with only one player. You have to kill 5 viruses before too many outbreaks occur and you lose. As you move around the map, random events happen on your ship that you have to deal with (don't fly into the Warp storms!). There is some research, but research is unimportant compared to XCOM because it just gives minor buffs and moves the plot along. All of the good gear is given as mission rewards and the progression feels better this way.

This is one of the highest quality and polished 40k games I've played, too. If only they were all this good.

There's so, so much I love about this game but when it comes to difficulty balancing it smacks of junior designers not understanding that you need players to leave your game wanting more, and not leaving frustrated. If I get the sequel it won't be until it is heavily discounted.

The game is just too hard, even on normal difficulty. It's grueling, unforgiving, and made in a way that if you don't optimize everything to the T, you're going to fail missions, and soon the whole campaign. At that point, you have to restart the entire campaign... 20-30h of gameplay down the drain. The game is so hard, that you'll have to save constantly, cause one small mistake could be fatal. There's absolutely no space for any sort of mistakes starting from about 1/3 of the game. If you're a masochist, you'll love this. Otherwise, maybe play it on Easy. I played on normal, and after restarting the same non-optional story mission 20 times, at about 1/3 of the way in the campaign, after 30h of play, I just gave up. I was not having any fun whatsoever, even thought I'm a pretty hardcore video game player.

Like XCOM 2: maintain a barracks of soldiers, improve your mobile HQ to better aid deployment options, a variety of classes

Differs from XCOM 2: Hit chance is always 100%, the RNG solely lies in the ability procs/crits - this however does not make it easy, as the crits and abilities are vital to success. In fact it is actually a nicely worked solution to XCOM 2's difficulty curve problem (where the start of your campaign is super difficult but the end game content is extremely easy as the RNG element is effectively made redundant). 

In Chaos Gate the challenge actually ramps up as the game progresses, although your tech/equipment/soldiers will improve over the campaign - an ever growing list of injuries and limited wargear will force you to make some tough decisions in terms of where, when and who to deploy on missions.

I sincerely hope that they expand this franchise by adding the other daemon races to the game (Khorne, Tzeench or Slaanesh) as I feel that would add an extra layer of tactical complexity to this game. Nurgle is typically known for slow-moving, tanky, attrition tactics - one of the other chaos gods could certainly provide some icing to this already delicious cake.

I didn't truly bounce off this tactics game (unlike "Miasma Chronicles,") but I did get stymied somewhere in the middle.

Which is a shame, because I ended up appreciating the cartoony visual style and highly entertaining sound design. Or at least, one part of it. The Space Marines sound like they weigh about 800 lbs, so when they're running at an opponent the thudding is tremendously satisfying.

Where I got stuck is that "Chaos Gate" seems to value two things: Aggression, and builds that maximize willpower and action point return. The aggression part I generally got a handle on. If there's a way to play this cautiously, which would be my usual, I can't figure it out. Taking your time is punished...but aggression is also punished a bit, because if you're really going for it you also push forward the timer for all kinds of negative effects to get applied.

Also, your Space Marines take quite a lot of damage in a big hurry. There are opponents that can fire a single energy blast and tear half the HP off a Marine unless they're in Terminator armor. (Plus, it seems like a single scratch causes a unit to return with a multi-day hit point penalty.)

This is where the builds come in. My understanding is that you really need to get everyone into Terminator armor as fast as you can, and then ignore everything that doesn't involve either permanently increasing WP and AP, or creating more of those points on the fly. If you didn't realize that going in, you may have just hamstrung yourself. I don't have a lot of love for games that say, "We'll provide you with a whole box of solutions, but there's only one real one," which seems to be the case here. I could be wrong! That's what it seemed like in the heat of the moment, though.

As such, I don't know if this game is really for me, although I might come back to it later.

Excellent TBS.  I have played this off and on throughout the years, never completing the game entirely.  Finally  I decided to turn up the difficulty and give it another shot.  I was not let down.

The game difficulty ramps up very quickly, a few mistakes can cost everything, the classes are unique and can have a variety of builds for each of the eight unique knight types.  The campaign missions, outside of the standard planetary 'bloom' operations, were fantastic.  Though quite long, being able to save mid mission is very helpful if you are struggling or need to take a break.

Yes the power fantasy of being a silver boy and slaying armies alone is lacking, but if you can ignore a few of the lore bits and just enjoy the game you won't be let down.  

That all being said, if you are new to TBS and do not understand the progression route you should take, the game would be quite long and likely feel entirely too repetitive.  So if you are new to TBS, let me recommend that you focus on the seed research tree to keep the game progressing quickly, and you will only be dealing with 1-3 repetitive bloom operations between unique campaign missions.

It is a shame this game was left behind, more DLC, weapons such as claw or fist would have been great, but as it stands this game is a great time and a single campaign is well recommended.  

8/10: Excellent TBS, Unique Classes and Equipment, Diversity in Squad Builds, great story with an awesome ending within the 40k universe

10/10: Replayability

8/10: Mostly Bug Free, a few hangups, and 1 crash during a 150hr (700+Day) Campaign

On one level, it's simply an XCOM2 clone with a 40k skin, but underneath that it's a game that has built on and refined what was learned from XCOM2.  Most of the things that were aggravatingly annoying about the XCOM games (miss chance, anyone?) are gone, but the enemies have enough mechanics and abilities to make the game still challenging and fun.

The only real negatives I can mention are that I DO NOT like that this remake replaces conventional Marines with the Grey Knights.  I think the game would have been stronger if it were some other Chapter thrown desperately into the fray rather than one SPECIFICALLY DESIGNED to fight JUST the foe that the game centers on...but that's a minor personal gripe, and no scratch on the game itself.

The overall design is just to always always annoy the player with lose or lose situations. I understand the  "make the best out of the worst situation kind of deal, but at some point it just get frustrating.

Between warpsurges, weird conversations that penalizes you no matter the choice, to missions spawning outside out of the range of your ship, you'll never get there in time. Yeah, okay...

Too bad, the art is really cool, loyal to the franchise, and reminiscent of the figurines.

This was  a pretty good game on launch. But the addition of the defend servitors missions is just plain awful! They are so unbelievably dull, and the game is clearly not designed to deal with them. It plays perfectly fine on my steam deck despite it saying unsupported. I really enjoy this game!

Getting back into the campaign was confusing, and the game quickly forced me into missions that felt overwhelmingly difficult.

I don’t mind a challenge, but this feels unbalanced. I constantly feel under equipped, with no real way to catch up. Progress often feels reversed.
